qs.e: A core pillar of Dicey's Rule of Law mandates that punishment or loss of rights can only follow a distinct violation of established law proven before regular courts.

qs.q:
Consider the federal governance structure illustrated below:
<svg width="280" height="90" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="background:#fff;"><rect x="90" y="10" width="100" height="25" fill="#fff" stroke="#000" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="140" y="27" font-size="10" text-anchor="middle">Federal Level</text><rect x="10" y="55" width="100" height="25" fill="#fff" stroke="#000" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="60" y="72" font-size="10" text-anchor="middle">State Level</text><rect x="170" y="55" width="100" height="25" fill="#fff" stroke="#000" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="220" y="72" font-size="10" text-anchor="middle">Local Level</text><path d="M 140 35 L 60 55 M 140 35 L 220 55" stroke="#000" stroke-width="1.5"/></svg>
Which arm of government holds the primary constitutional duty of interpreting the jurisdictional boundaries of these tiers?
qs.e: The Judiciary interprets the constitution and resolves jurisdictional disputes between federal, state, and local tiers of government in a federation.

qs.q: In a presidential democracy, the Chief Executive serves concurrently as
o: Head of State and Head of Government
Head of State and Chief Justice of the Federation
Head of Government and Speaker of Parliament
President of the Senate and Cabinet Secretary
qs.e: Under presidential democracy, executive power is unified in a single President who performs ceremonial functions (Head of State) and executes administration (Head of Government).

qs.q: The power of the executive head to officially grant pardons or reduce sentences for convicted criminal offenders is known as the
qs.e: The prerogative of mercy allows the President or State Governor to grant pardons or commute judicial sentences on recommendation of an advisory council.

qs.q: A traditional ruler commands compliance based on custom, ancestry, and cultural lineage. In Max Weber's political classification, this authority is described as
qs.e: Max Weber defined traditional authority as legitimacy derived from established customs, hereditary rights, and traditional beliefs passed down through generations.

qs.q: A state policy that encourages private enterprise, free market competition, individual property ownership, and constitutional checks on state power is rooted in
qs.e: Liberalism promotes individual liberties, protection of private property, free market mechanisms, and constitutional limits on state intervention.

qs.q: If amending a constitutional provision requires a two-thirds majority in both houses of the national assembly plus approval by resolution of two-thirds of state legislatures, the constitution is
qs.e: Rigid constitutions prescribe strict, supermajority amendment procedures involving national and sub-national legislatures to prevent easy alterations.

qs.q: Section 308 of the 1999 Nigerian Constitution protects incumbent Governors and the President from civil or criminal proceedings during tenure. This provision represents
o: A constitutional limitation to absolute equality before the law
An enforcement of the doctrine of ultra vires
A statutory application of delegated legislation
qs.e: Executive immunity under Section 308 shields chief executives from prosecution while in office to maintain governance stability, representing a constitutional exception to universal equality before the law.

qs.q: In a cabinet system of government, executive ministers are chosen from among elected members of the legislature. This structural arrangement is termed
qs.e: In cabinet (parliamentary) governance, ministers hold seats in parliament, creating a fusion of executive and legislative personnel.

qs.q: During the passage of a legislative bill, detailed clause-by-clause analysis, expert submissions, and proposed amendments occur during the
qs.e: The Committee stage allows legislative committees to examine bill provisions thoroughly, conduct public hearings, and insert detailed amendments.

qs.q: Under the 1999 Constitution of Nigeria, the Supreme Court exercises original jurisdiction in legal disputes arising between
o: The Federation and a State, or between federating States
Commercial banks and private corporate entities
Civil service unions and federal ministries
Local government chairmen and municipal contractors
qs.e: Section 232 of the 1999 Constitution vests original jurisdiction in the Supreme Court for legal disputes between the Federal Government and States, or among States.

qs.q: Which of the following matters is contained on the Exclusive Legislative List of the Federal National Assembly of Nigeria?
o: Defense, aviation, customs duties, and currency
Establishment of municipal markets and street naming
Local chieftancy disputes and customary land tenure
qs.e: Defense, currency, customs, and aviation fall under the Exclusive Legislative List, meaning only the federal legislature can make laws regarding them.

qs.q: The colonial constitution that introduced the Elective Principle into Nigerian politics in 1922 was the
qs.e: The 1922 Clifford Constitution introduced the elective principle, granting 4 elected seats (3 for Lagos, 1 for Calabar) in the Legislative Council.

qs.q: The Nigerian National Democratic Party (NNDP), founded in 1923 by Herbert Macaulay, was primarily formed to contest elections established under the
qs.e: Macaulay formed the NNDP in 1923 to field candidates for the newly elective seats created under Sir Hugh Clifford's 1922 constitution.

qs.q: An organization such as the Nigeria Union of Teachers (NUT) or the Nigerian Bar Association (NBA) acts as what class of pressure group?
qs.e: The NUT and NBA represent occupational/professional groups that unite practitioners to defend economic and professional interests.

qs.q: Under the First-Past-The-Post electoral system, the candidate declared elected is the one who achieves
o: The highest number of valid votes cast in the contest
An absolute majority exceeding 75% of total registered voters
Unanimous endorsement from all political party delegates
At least half of the total votes cast in every polling unit
qs.e: In First-Past-The-Post (plurality system), the candidate with the highest single tally of valid votes wins, even if it falls short of an absolute majority.

qs.q: Citizens in State Z comply with government directives primarily because they believe the political system acquired power through legitimate constitutional processes. This compliance is based on
qs.e: Political legitimacy exists when citizens recognize the government's rightful authority to rule based on adherence to established legal and constitutional norms.

qs.q: A research study reveals that citizens in Region W have high awareness of government outputs like taxation, but exhibit minimal active participation in input activities like voting or policy debate. Almond and Verba classify this political culture as
qs.e: Subject political culture features awareness of governmental outputs (laws, taxes) but passive involvement in shaping government policies or participating in input mechanisms.

qs.q: A state system where major heavy industries, railways, and utilities are state-owned, while small retail enterprises operate under private ownership with state social welfare programs, is a
qs.e: Democratic socialism or a mixed economy balances public ownership of core infrastructure and utilities with regulated private ownership in retail and service sectors.

qs.q: The fundamental doctrine of constitutionalism requires that
o: Government authority is strictly limited by constitutional law to protect individual liberties
The executive arm can suspend legislative statutes during economic recessions
The legislature holds absolute power to amend basic human rights without oversight
Judges are appointed solely by the parliamentary leader of the ruling party
qs.e: Constitutionalism maintains that government power must be legally constrained by constitutional principles to prevent arbitrary rule and safeguard civil rights.

qs.q: A foreign diplomat stationed in Abuja commits an infraction but is exempt from domestic criminal trial under international legal accords. This exemption illustrates
o: A limitation to the strict application of the rule of law
An operational application of delegated legislation
qs.e: Diplomatic immunity protects foreign accredited diplomats from local prosecution, serving as a recognized legal exception to universal rule of law application.

qs.q: When the President refuses assent to a bill, and the National Assembly re-passes the bill by a two-thirds majority in both chambers to enact it into law, this demonstrates
o: Checks and balances over executive veto power
qs.e: Overriding executive vetoes by supermajority legislative votes is a classic checks-and-balances mechanism to prevent executive obstruction of legislative will.

qs.q: The adoption of bicameralism in federal states like Nigeria is primarily intended to
o: Provide equal state representation in the upper chamber while accommodating population differences in the lower chamber
Accelerate the passage of bills by bypassing committee reviews
Reduce overall costs associated with legislative salaries and logistics
Prevent judicial review of acts passed by the federal assembly
qs.e: Bicameralism in federations balances regional equality (equal Senate seats for each state) with demographic representation (proportional House of Representatives seats).

qs.q: In a cabinet system, the constitutional rule of collective responsibility requires that
o: Cabinet ministers must publicly endorse all government decisions or resign if they publicly dissent
Ministers are individually tried by the supreme court for cabinet policy failures
Civil servants share criminal liability for cabinet executive decrees
Opposition parties in parliament must vote for cabinet monetary budgets
qs.e: Collective responsibility obligates cabinet members to support all cabinet decisions publicly. A minister who cannot defend a cabinet policy is expected to resign.

qs.q: The legal doctrine of *Stare Decisis* mandates that lower courts must
o: Abide by legal precedents established in judgments of higher appellate courts
Submit constitutional disputes to executive referendum before ruling
Disregard statutory enactments lacking unanimous parliamentary consent
Re-examine all criminal judgments issued by international bodies
qs.e: Stare Decisis obligates lower courts to follow binding legal principles (precedents) set by superior appellate courts in earlier similar cases.

qs.q: If a state law conflicts with a valid federal enactment on a Concurrent Legislative List item in Nigeria, the outcome is governed by the
o: Doctrine of Inconsistency, making the state law void to the extent of conflict
Principle of State Autonomy, overriding federal legislation
Supreme Court administrative circular nullifying both laws
qs.e: Under Section 4(5) of the 1999 Constitution, the Doctrine of Inconsistency voids state law to the extent that it conflicts with valid federal law on concurrent items.

qs.q: The 1963 Republican Constitution of Nigeria altered the judicial system by
o: Abolishing appeals to the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council and making the Supreme Court of Nigeria the final apex court
Establishing regional military tribunals to replace state high courts
Conferring ultimate judicial review authority on the Prime Minister
Transferring appointment of judges to state legislative speakers
qs.e: The 1963 Republican Constitution severed judicial ties with Britain by replacing the Privy Council with the Nigerian Supreme Court as the final court of appeal.

qs.q: The Action Group (AG) formed in 1951 evolved from which socio-cultural organization?
qs.e: The Action Group evolved from Egbe Omo Oduduwa, a Yoruba cultural organization, to contest elections under the 1951 Macpherson Constitution.

qs.q: When a trade union orders a general strike to force government implementation of a signed labor agreement, it is using
qs.e: Strikes are direct industrial actions employed by unions to exert coercive pressure on employers or governments to resolve industrial grievances.

qs.q: Redrawing electoral district boundaries deliberately to maximize seats for a ruling party while diluting opposition votes is called
qs.e: Gerrymandering is the manipulative alteration of constituency boundaries to secure unfair electoral advantages for a specific party.

qs.q: Privatization of public enterprises differs from commercialization in that privatization involves
o: Transferring equity ownership and management control of state assets to private buyers
Retaining 100% government ownership while eliminating operational subsidies
Converting state corporations directly into government executive ministries
Abolishing corporate tax liability for foreign industrial investors
qs.e: Privatization transfers ownership shares and control of government enterprises to private owners, unlike commercialization which keeps state ownership intact.

qs.q: In political analysis, a major limitation to national sovereignty in contemporary international relations occurs when a state
o: Signs binding international treaties that restrict its domestic policy choices
Enacts internal criminal laws through its elected national legislature
Establishes municipal local councils to manage refuse collection
Appoints judicial officers to hear disputes between local citizens
qs.e: Voluntary international treaties and membership in international organizations restrict a state's complete freedom of action, acting as legal limits on absolute external sovereignty.

qs.q: A key distinction between Western Democratic Socialism and Classical Marxist Communism is that Democratic Socialism
o: Seeks social equality and welfare reforms through constitutional democratic processes rather than violent revolution
Advocates complete total state ownership of all personal property and private clothing
Rejects multiparty democratic elections in favor of a permanent military dictatorship
Abolishes legislative parliaments and replaces them with worker soviets
qs.e: Democratic Socialism aims to achieve equitable wealth distribution through democratic parliamentary means and welfare policy, whereas Marxism-Leninism advocates revolutionary overthrow of capitalism.

qs.q: The primary objective of incorporating a Bill of Rights into a written constitution is to
o: Protect individual fundamental freedoms against executive or legislative encroachment
Enable the executive to suspend legal trials during economic downturns
Grant permanent judicial immunity to legislative committee chairmen
Ensure that state governors can override federal court rulings
qs.e: Entrenching a Bill of Rights in a constitution guarantees civil liberties against government overreach, providing legal remedies when rights are violated.

qs.q: Administrative tribunals created to resolve specialized civil or labor disputes are often viewed as potential challenges to strict Rule of Law because they
o: May lack the formal procedural safeguards and judicial independence of regular courts
Operate under direct supervision of municipal police commissioners
Are prohibited from issuing written judgments or hearing legal counsel
Require unanimous legislative confirmation for every ruling
qs.e: Administrative tribunals may be headed by executive officials or lack full judicial independence and standard evidence rules, creating exceptions to Dicey's ideal of regular court jurisdiction.

qs.q: Delegated legislation is frequently criticized in constitutional law because it
o: Allows non-elected administrative bodies to exercise lawmaking powers with reduced parliamentary scrutiny
Transfers judicial appellate authority directly to executive cabinet ministers
Requires all administrative rules to be subjected to national referendums
Prevents statutory bodies from collecting municipal utility tariffs
qs.e: Delegated legislation empowers executive departments to make rules (statutory instruments), which can undermine parliamentary supremacy if not adequately supervised.

qs.q: In parliamentary governance, if the House of Commons passes a formal vote of no confidence against the Prime Minister, the constitutional outcome is that
o: The Prime Minister and Cabinet must resign or dissolve parliament for fresh general elections
The Supreme Court automatically assumes temporary executive control of the state
The Speaker of Parliament becomes Chief Executive for a six-year term
The cabinet ministers continue in office while the Prime Minister alone is replaced
qs.e: A successful vote of no confidence forces the government (Prime Minister and Cabinet) to resign or seek a parliamentary dissolution to hold new elections.

qs.q: The National Judicial Council (NJC) in Nigeria safeguards judicial independence primarily by
o: Controlling recommendations for appointment, discipline, and retirement of judicial officers independently of political party dictates
Formulating federal tax legislation for legislative debate
Commanding police officers during election dispute enforcement
Overriding Supreme Court decisions through administrative rulings
qs.e: The NJC handles recruitment, promotion, and disciplinary control of judges, removing executive political influence from judicial appointments and security of tenure.

qs.q: Under Nigerian fiscal federalism, the principle of Derivation in revenue allocation dictates that
o: A proportion of federally collected revenue from natural resources is returned to the specific state of extraction
All national revenues are distributed equally among local government councils regardless of location
State governments retain 100% of commercial taxes while central government receives foreign aid
Landlocked states receive higher budgetary allocations than coastal states
qs.e: Derivation allocates a specific percentage of revenue generated from natural resources (e.g. oil) back to the specific states where those resources were extracted.

qs.q: The 1954 Lyttelton Constitution was a watershed in Nigerian political history primarily because it
o: Established a formal federal structure with regional civil services, judicial regionalization, and premier offices
Abolished all regional legislatures and consolidated power under a unitary governor-general
Introduced universal adult suffrage across all Northern provinces for the first time
Created a executive presidency modeled after the United States constitution
qs.e: The Lyttelton Constitution established true federalism in Nigeria, creating autonomous regions, regional civil services, regional judiciaries, and Premier posts.

qs.q: In the Nigerian Second Republic (1979–1983), the election of Alhaji Shehu Shagari was challenged at the Supreme Court in *Awolowo v. Shagari* primarily over the interpretation of
o: What constituted two-thirds of the nineteen states of the federation
Whether civil servants could contest presidential elections without resigning
The legality of campaign financing by foreign trade organizations
The constitutional status of the Federal Capital Territory Abuja
qs.e: The legal battle centered on whether winning 25% in 12 states plus 19.6% in Kano State satisfied the constitutional requirement of winning 25% of votes in two-thirds of 19 states (12 2/3 states).

qs.q: The 1988 Civil Service Reform in Nigeria under General Ibrahim Babangida radically restructured ministry management by
o: Designating the Minister as the Chief Executive and Accounting Officer while changing Permanent Secretaries to political Directors-General
Abolishing all administrative classes and placing ministries under military commanders
Transferring civil service recruitment directly to private employment agencies
Granting permanent tenure immunity to all civil service clerks
qs.e: The 1988 reform made Ministers accounting officers (replacing Permanent Secretaries) and political appointees titled Directors-General, politicizing top civil service positions.

qs.q: Analyze the legal tension between Section 305 (State of Emergency powers) and Chapter IV (Fundamental Rights) under the 1999 Nigerian Constitution. During a validly declared state of emergency, executive emergency regulations may derogate from certain fundamental rights EXCEPT the right to
o: Life and freedom from torture or inhuman treatment
qs.e: Even during emergency declarations under constitutional law and international human rights conventions, non-derogable rights such as the right to life and freedom from torture cannot be suspended.

qs.q: Evaluate the application of the 'Doctrine of Covering the Field' in Nigerian constitutional law when both National Assembly and State House of Assembly pass valid legislation on a concurrent item. If the federal enactment comprehensively covers the legislative area, the state law becomes
o: Inoperative and dormant because the federal law covers the entire field, even if there is no direct inconsistency
Automatically converted into a municipal bye-law enforced by local police
Elevated to a constitutional amendment requiring Supreme Court ratification
Validly applicable within state borders while federal law applies in federal territories
qs.e: Under Covering the Field, where federal law manifests an intention to cover an entire subject matter exhaustively, state law on that subject becomes inoperative/dormant, regardless of whether direct contradiction exists.

qs.q: Compare the 1922 Clifford Constitution with the 1946 Richards Constitution regarding nationalist criticism. Nationalist leaders opposed the 1946 Richards Constitution despite its regional representation because it
o: Was promulgated without prior consultation with Nigerian leaders and maintained an unofficial majority of nominated chiefs
Abolished the elective principle introduced in 1922 for Lagos and Calabar
Merged Nigeria into a unitary administration governed directly from London
Prohibited Nigerian political parties from publishing newspapers
qs.e: Nationalists criticized the Richards Constitution for lack of popular consultation (it was imposed from above) and because official/nominated chiefs dominated regional houses, keeping real power with colonial authorities.

qs.q: Assess the constitutional impact of the 1976 Local Government Reform on intergovernmental relations in Nigeria. The reform altered local governance by
o: Entrenching local government as a recognized third tier of government with direct statutory allocations from the Federation Account
Subordinating local councils entirely to traditional rulers who held sole executive veto
Abolishing elected local council chairmen in favor of appointed military sole administrators
Dividing local governance into 36 state-controlled private municipal companies
qs.e: The 1976 reform elevated local government to an autonomous third tier of federal governance with constitutional recognition, standardized powers, and statutory financial allocations.

qs.q: Critique the implementation of the Federal Character Principle under Section 14(3) of the 1999 Constitution of Nigeria. While intended to promote national unity and prevent regional domination, critics argue that in practice it often
o: Subordinates meritocracy in public service appointments to geopolitical quota considerations
Eliminates state representation in federal ministerial appointments
Transfers executive hiring decisions to international civil service commissions
Prevents citizens from taking up residence in states other than their state of origin
qs.e: The Federal Character Principle mandates equitable representation of all states in public institutions, but critics contend that strict quota adherence can compromise meritocracy and administrative competence.

qs.q: The complex process through which individuals acquire political beliefs, values, civic attitudes, and knowledge about their political system is known as
qs.e: Political socialization is the lifelong process by which individuals learn and internalize political attitudes, values, and civic norms through agents like family, school, and media.

qs.q: A system of government in which supreme political authority is concentrated in a single central government with no constitutionally autonomous regional states is
qs.e: In a unitary system, all constitutional authority resides in the central national government, which may delegate administrative powers to sub-national units at its pleasure.

qs.q: Which doctrine formulated by Montesquieu asserts that executive, legislative, and judicial powers should be exercised by separate governmental organs?
qs.e: Baron de Montesquieu advocated the separation of powers into three independent branches (legislative, executive, judicial) to prevent tyranny and safeguard liberty.

qs.q: In a unicameral legislative system, the national parliament consists of
qs.e: Unicameralism describes a parliamentary structure composed of only one legislative body or house.

qs.q: A person who is a Nigerian citizen by birth acquires citizenship of another nation. Under Section 28 of the 1999 Nigerian Constitution, this person
o: Retains Nigerian citizenship because dual citizenship is allowed for citizens by birth
Must be deported to their country of birth
Requires annual clearance from the Senate to retain passport
qs.e: Section 28 permits dual citizenship for persons who are Nigerian citizens by birth, meaning foreign citizenship acquisition does not strip them of Nigerian citizenship.

qs.q: Nigeria's flagship foreign policy initiative launched in 1987 to provide technical expertise and skilled manpower to developing African, Caribbean, and Pacific countries is the
qs.e: The Technical Aid Corps (TAC) scheme was established by Nigeria in 1987 as a foreign policy tool to share technical expertise with developing ACP nations.

qs.q: Political culture is best defined as the pattern of individual attitudes, values, orientations, and beliefs toward the political system held by
o: Members of a political community or nation
Military officers serving in junta councils
qs.e: Political culture encompasses the collective attitudes, values, and emotional orientations of citizens toward governance, authority, and political institutions.

qs.q: Which political ideology advocates traditional social stability, preservation of established institutions, organic social order, and gradual incremental change rather than radical reform?
qs.e: Conservatism emphasizes respect for established political institutions, social tradition, order, and incremental constitutional evolution over revolutionary change.

qs.q: An unwritten constitution relies heavily on which source of constitutional authority alongside statutory enactments?
qs.e: Unwritten constitutions (such as Britain's) draw core rules from constitutional conventions, historical statutes, judicial precedents, and customary practices.

qs.q: Laws made by administrative bodies or executive agencies under authority delegated to them by the legislature are known as
qs.e: Delegated legislation (statutory instruments, orders-in-council, bye-laws) consists of rules made by executive departments under statutory authority granted by parliament.

qs.q: In a pure parliamentary system, if the Prime Minister loses support of the parliamentary majority, executive authority is restructured through
o: A vote of no confidence leading to cabinet resignation or parliamentary dissolution
An immediate military coup overseen by the supreme court
Direct appointment of a foreign governor-general by international treaty
A presidential executive order suspending parliament
qs.e: Loss of majority support in parliament triggers a vote of no confidence, forcing the Prime Minister and Cabinet to resign or call fresh elections.

qs.q: The primary role of Election Petition Tribunals in Nigeria's judicial hierarchy is to
o: Adjudicate disputes and challenges arising from the conduct of general elections
Draft electoral guidelines for political party primary elections
Formulate national revenue allocation formulas for state governments
Register political parties for national elections
qs.e: Election Petition Tribunals are specialized judicial bodies constituted after elections to hear and determine petitions challenging election outcomes.

qs.q: The power of federal courts to declare acts of the legislature or executive unconstitutional and null and void is called
qs.e: Judicial review is the authority of courts to examine government actions and statutory laws to determine whether they conform to constitutional provisions.

qs.q: Under the 1999 Constitution of Nigeria, residual powers—matters not listed on either the Exclusive or Concurrent Lists—belong exclusively to
qs.e: Residual powers in the 1999 Constitution belong to state governments, covering matters not explicitly assigned to federal jurisdiction on the Exclusive or Concurrent lists.

qs.q: The 1946 Richards Constitution was significant in Nigerian constitutional history primarily because it
o: Introduced regionalism by establishing Regional Houses of Assembly for North, West, and East
Created an executive presidential system with a two-chamber parliament
Abolished the office of the colonial Governor-General
Granted complete independence to Northern Nigeria
qs.e: The 1946 Richards Constitution introduced formal regionalism, dividing Nigeria into Northern, Western, and Eastern regions with regional legislative assemblies.

qs.q: In the Nigerian First Republic, which political party formed the central coalition government with the Northern People's Congress (NPC)?
qs.e: The NCNC, led by Nnamdi Azikiwe, formed a federal coalition government with the NPC led by Sir Abubakar Tafawa Balewa following the 1959 federal elections.

qs.q: A pressure group whose primary objective is to promote a selfless moral cause, human rights, or public welfare rather than financial gain for members is a
qs.e: Promotional (or cause) groups (such as human rights bodies or environmental protection organizations) campaign for broader public interests rather than narrow material self-interest.

qs.q: The independent electoral body responsible for organizing, supervising, and conducting federal and state elections in Nigeria is
qs.e: INEC is the statutory constitutional agency empowered under Section 153 to conduct presidential, legislative, and governorship elections across Nigeria.

qs.q: In a state where citizens participate directly in voting on specific policy proposals and legislative referendums rather than relying solely on elected representatives, the system is
qs.e: Direct democracy enables citizens to vote directly on laws and policy decisions (via referendums/plebiscites) rather than delegating all decisions to elected representatives.

qs.q: Traditional African Communalism differs from Western Marxist Communism primarily because Communalism was based on
o: Cooperative community land ownership and shared social duty without industrial class warfare theories
State-enforced military collectivization of heavy urban factories
Dictatorship of industrial trade unions over agrarian peasants
Total elimination of family structures and cultural chieftaincies
qs.e: African Communalism emphasized family land ownership, mutual community assistance, and social solidarity without the dialectical materialism or industrial class warfare central to Marxism.

qs.q: A rigid constitution is advantageous in a multi-ethnic federation primarily because it
o: Protects minority rights and federating state autonomy against arbitrary altering by dominant majorities
Allows the President to suspend fundamental rights without parliamentary approval
Enables quick legislative changes during minor economic fluctuations
Eliminates the requirement for judicial review of federal laws
qs.e: Rigid constitutions ensure that federal terms and minority protections cannot be unilaterally changed by temporary parliamentary majorities.

qs.q: The legal remedy of *Habeas Corpus* serves as a crucial safeguard under the Rule of Law by empowering courts to
o: Command an authority detaining a person to produce them in court to show legal cause for detention
Override statutory enactments passed by state legislative houses
Impeach elected executive governors for financial misconduct
Appoint administrative heads of government ministries
qs.e: The writ of Habeas Corpus requires detaining authorities to bring a prisoner to court and justify the legal grounds for detention, protecting individuals from unlawful arrest.

qs.q: The system of checks and balances operates in a presidential democracy to ensure that
o: Each branch of government possesses explicit constitutional mechanisms to monitor and restrain the powers of the other branches
The executive arm exercises exclusive authority over legislative budgets and judicial trials
The legislature can remove judges without constitutional investigation or trial
State governors command federal military formations during civil protests
qs.e: Checks and balances give each arm specific constitutional tools (veto, veto override, judicial review, appointment confirmation) to limit potential abuse of power by other arms.

qs.q: The Power of the Purse held by the legislature refers to its constitutional authority to
o: Authorize government expenditure, approve annual budgetary appropriations, and levy public taxes
Mint foreign currency and regulate commercial bank interest rates
Audit private corporate balance sheets for stock market listing
Direct central bank foreign reserve disbursements without executive submission
qs.e: Power of the purse is the legislative power to control public spending and taxation; executive departments cannot spend public money without legislative budgetary approval.

qs.q: In a presidential system, the Cabinet Ministers are directly accountable to
o: The Speaker of the House of Representatives
qs.e: In a presidential system, ministers serve at the pleasure of the President who appoints and can remove them, making them individually accountable to the President.

qs.q: Which of the following bodies is empowered to discipline and recommend the removal of judicial officers in Nigeria?
qs.e: The NJC has constitutional authority to investigate judicial misconduct and recommend the discipline or removal of judges to the President or State Governors.

qs.q: Fiscal federalism in Nigeria centers primarily on the contentious issue of
o: Designing equitable formulas for revenue allocation among federal, state, and local tiers
Determining the official national currency exchange rate for foreign imports
Selecting military officers to command state security task forces
Allocating university admissions quotas among private secondary schools
qs.e: Fiscal federalism involves financial relations between tiers of government, specifically how revenue collected into the Federation Account is shared vertically and horizontally.

qs.q: The 1951 Macpherson Constitution was notable for introducing which major executive feature at the central level?
o: A Council of Ministers with Nigerian ministers holding supervisory roles
An executive presidency elected through direct universal suffrage
A supreme military ruling council with legislative decree powers
A ceremonial governor-general appointed by the regional premier
qs.e: The Macpherson Constitution introduced a central Council of Ministers comprising colonial officials and 12 Nigerian ministers (4 from each region), granting Nigerians executive ministerial roles.

qs.q: During the Third Republic transition under General Ibrahim Babangida, which two political parties were officially created by government decree?
o: Social Democratic Party (SDP) and National Republican Convention (NRC)
People's Democratic Party (PDP) and All Progressives Congress (APC)
Action Group (AG) and Northern People's Congress (NPC)
Unity Party of Nigeria (UPN) and National Party of Nigeria (NPN)
qs.e: The Babangida military regime established a statutory two-party system, creating the SDP ('a little to the left') and NRC ('a little to the right').

qs.q: An anomic pressure group is characterized by
o: Spontaneous, unorganized crowd demonstrations or riots arising from sudden collective frustration
Formal corporate organization with permanent offices and legal advisors
Professional membership guidelines enforced through state registration
Secret lobbying activities conducted inside legislative committee rooms
qs.e: Anomic pressure groups emerge spontaneously in response to sudden events or crises, taking the form of unorganized protests, riots, or flash demonstrations without formal structure.

qs.q: Proportional Representation is an electoral system designed to
o: Allocate legislative seats to political parties in direct proportion to the percentage of total votes they receive nationally
Ensure that only the largest political party wins all seats in parliament
Require candidates to secure a 100% unanimous vote in their local constituencies
Restrict voting rights exclusively to landowning property holders
qs.e: Proportional Representation awards legislative seats based on the proportion of votes a party wins, ensuring minority parties gain representation reflective of popular support.

qs.q: Public corporations are established by Acts of Parliament primarily to
o: Provide essential public utilities and services with commercial flexibility while serving public interest
Execute civil service administrative queries for ministry clerks
Draft electoral guidelines for political party convention voting
Appoint appellate judges to state customary courts of appeal
qs.e: Public corporations are statutory bodies created to operate essential utilities or commercial operations efficiently while serving public policy goals outside strict civil service bureaucracy.

qs.q: The principle of civil service permanence ensures that civil servants
o: Maintain security of employment across changing political administrations and elected governments
Hold office for life without possibility of retirement or resignation
Are immune from criminal prosecution for civil fraud
Receive salary increases automatically whenever national inflation rises
qs.e: Permanence means career civil servants retain their jobs despite changes in political leadership, providing administrative continuity between outgoing and incoming governments.

qs.q: A major distinction between legal sovereignty and political sovereignty is that legal sovereignty resides in
o: The supreme law-making body whose enactments courts enforce, whereas political sovereignty resides in the electorate
The armed forces during civil strife, whereas political sovereignty resides in judicial tribunals
Foreign international courts, whereas political sovereignty resides in municipal local councils
State executive governors, whereas political sovereignty resides in traditional chiefs
qs.e: Legal sovereignty is the ultimate lawmaking power recognized by law (e.g. Parliament), while political sovereignty lies with the electorate whose votes ultimately determine who holds power.

qs.q: An essential characteristic of Fascism that distinguishes it from Constitutional Liberalism is its
o: Totalitarian subordination of individual rights to the absolute power and glory of the state
Enforcement of universal adult suffrage in transparent multiparty elections
Protection of judicial independence and habeas corpus rights
Devolution of fiscal authority to autonomous regional councils
qs.e: Fascism rejects liberal individualism and constitutionalism, demanding complete subordination of the citizen to an all-powerful totalitarian state led by a dictator.

qs.q: Constitutional conventions play a critical role in unwritten constitutional governance because they
o: Represent unwritten political rules of conduct that regulate executive and parliamentary behavior through long usage
Provide binding military decrees enforced by armed state police
Enable private commercial corporations to enact statutory laws
Allow local government councils to veto national assembly acts
qs.e: Conventions are non-codified practices accepted as binding political rules of constitutional behavior (e.g. Prime Minister resigning after losing a vote of no confidence).

qs.q: In administrative law, the *Ultra Vires* doctrine empowers courts to invalidate actions of public authorities if the authority has
o: Exceeded the legal powers explicitly conferred on it by statutory legislation
Failed to secure unanimous endorsement from political party executives
Implemented a policy without publishing it in foreign press outlets
Appointed civil servants without university degrees
qs.e: Ultra vires ('beyond powers') means an administrative body acted beyond its statutory authority, rendering the action legally void.

qs.q: Legislative oversight over executive agencies is executed primarily through
o: Public hearings, budgetary scrutiny, and committee investigations of executive performance
Direct military command of executive department personnel
Drafting judicial appellate rulings for supreme court judges
qs.e: Legislative oversight uses committee investigations, budget reviews, and public hearings to hold executive ministries accountable for policy execution.

qs.q: The main structural weakness of a Confederal System compared to a Federal System is that the central confederal government
o: Lacks direct authority over individual citizens and depends entirely on voluntary cooperation of sovereign member states
Possesses absolute dictatorial power over regional legislative assemblies
Imposes uniform federal taxes without regional approval
Appoints all regional governors and judicial officers
qs.e: In a confederation, sovereignty remains with constituent states; the central authority is weak and relies on member state consent, making it prone to instability or dissolution.

qs.q: The 1979 Constitution of Nigeria marked a fundamental departure from the 1960 and 1963 constitutions by establishing
o: An executive presidential system replacing the parliamentary cabinet system
A unicameral national assembly led by a military commander
A unitary administration that abolished all state governments
A constitutional monarchy headed by traditional rulers
qs.e: The 1979 Constitution introduced an executive presidential system modeled after the United States, departing from the parliamentary cabinet model of 1960/1963.

qs.q: The main constitutional problem associated with the State Joint Local Government Account (SJLGA) in Nigeria is that it
o: Enables state governments to divert or control federal statutory allocations meant for local councils
Prevents local government councils from levying market stall rates
Requires local councils to submit foreign trade treaties to the central bank
Transfers local council policing powers directly to federal military units
qs.e: Section 162(6) created the State Joint Local Government Account, which state governments frequently exploit to intercept and withhold statutory allocations intended for local councils.

qs.q: Nigeria's military intervention under ECOMOG in the Liberian Civil War (1990) was legally grounded in the foreign policy commitment to
o: Regional peace, security stabilization, and non-indifference to civilian suffering within West Africa
Expanding Nigerian territorial boundaries into neighboring West African states
Enforcing global maritime tariffs on foreign cargo vessels
Securing exclusive foreign mineral extraction rights in West Africa
qs.e: ECOMOG peace-enforcement in Liberia reflected Nigeria's leadership role in West Africa to stop human tragedy, restore regional security, and stabilize the sub-region.

qs.q: In the United Nations Security Council, a decision on non-procedural substantive matters requires nine affirmative votes including
o: Concurring votes of all five permanent members
Unanimous approval of all 193 member states of the General Assembly
Approval from the President of the International Court of Justice
A simple majority of non-permanent members only
qs.e: Under Article 27 of the UN Charter, substantive resolutions require 9 votes including concurring votes (or abstention without veto) of the 5 permanent members (P5).

qs.q: Evaluate the concept of Popular Sovereignty in democratic theory. Under this doctrine, ultimate political authority resides in
o: The people or electorate, who delegate power to government through periodic free elections
The hereditary monarch, whose decree is legally supreme over all citizens
The apex judicial court, which possesses absolute veto over legislative bills
The standing military junta, which controls sovereign instruments of violence
qs.e: Popular sovereignty posits that legitimate government authority originates from the consent of the governed (the people), exercised through constitutional democratic franchise.

qs.q: Synthesize the impact of judicial review on legislative supremacy in a federal presidential state. Unlike parliamentary systems with legislative supremacy, judicial review in a constitutional presidential system
o: Subordinates legislative enactments to constitutional standards, empowering courts to nullify unconstitutional statutes
Prohibits judges from interpreting statutory legislation passed by supermajorities
Requires the legislature to confirm every judicial verdict before execution
Grants cabinet ministers authority to dissolve supreme court benches
qs.e: In a constitutional presidential system with a written constitution, judicial review ensures constitutional supremacy, allowing courts to strike down invalid legislative acts.

qs.q: Analyze the structural flaw of the 1951 Macpherson Constitution that contributed to its rapid breakdown by 1953. The constitution failed primarily because
o: Central ministers owed primary political allegiance to their regional party leaders rather than to a unified central cabinet leadership
It created a unitary state that abolished all regional legislative assemblies
It denied Nigerians any representation in the central legislative house
It placed executive military command under regional traditional rulers
qs.e: Under Macpherson's constitution, central ministers were selected by regional assemblies and remained loyal to regional party leaders (Awolowo, Azikiwe, Ahmadu Bello), causing severe central cabinet friction.

qs.q: Critique the role of the Civil Service Commission under the 1999 Constitution. While designed as an independent body to manage public service personnel, its operational effectiveness is often compromised by
o: Political executive patronage in appointments and bureaucratic resistance to merit-based reforms
Direct legislative veto over individual civil service recruitment decisions
Supreme Court administrative directives restricting civil service promotions
Complete financial independence from state budgetary allocations
qs.e: Executive patronage, political interference, and entrenched bureaucratic inertia often undermine the Civil Service Commission's capacity to enforce strict meritocracy.

qs.q: Analyze the legal significance of the 2002 International Court of Justice (ICJ) ruling on the Bakassi Peninsula dispute between Nigeria and Cameroon. The ICJ awarded Bakassi to Cameroon primarily based on
o: The Anglo-German Treaty of 1913 establishing colonial boundaries, which Nigeria was obligated to respect under international law
Military occupation of the territory by Cameroonian armed forces during the 1990s
A national referendum conducted among Bakassi residents voting for Cameroonian citizenship
An executive resolution passed by the Organization of African Unity in 1963
qs.e: The ICJ judgment relied on the 1913 Anglo-German agreement demarcating colonial boundaries, upholding the principle of *uti possidetis juris* (respecting colonial borders upon independence).

qs.q: The fundamental legal status that confers full political rights, civic duties, and legal privileges upon an individual within a sovereign state is known as
qs.e: Citizenship is the legal status that links an individual to a sovereign state, granting civil and political rights alongside civic obligations.

qs.q: Which major organ of the United Nations is composed of all member states, with each state having one vote in global policy discussions?
qs.e: The UN General Assembly is the main deliberative organ where all 193 member states have equal representation and voting rights.

qs.q: The first military coup d'état in post-independence Nigeria occurred on
qs.e: Nigeria's first military coup occurred on January 15, 1966, led by young army majors (including Chukwuma Nzeogwu) and resulted in General Ironsi assuming power.

qs.q: Under a presidential constitution, the power to pass an annual appropriation bill authorizing federal government expenditure resides in the
qs.e: The legislature holds the 'power of the purse', meaning only the National Assembly can pass appropriation bills authorizing government spending.

qs.q:
Consider the lawmaking progression shown below:
<svg width="300" height="70" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="background:#fff;"><rect x="10" y="20" width="80" height="30" fill="#fff" stroke="#000" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="50" y="38" font-size="9" text-anchor="middle">First Reading</text><rect x="110" y="20" width="80" height="30" fill="#fff" stroke="#000" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="150" y="38" font-size="9" text-anchor="middle">Committee Stage</text><rect x="210" y="20" width="80" height="30" fill="#fff" stroke="#000" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="250" y="38" font-size="9" text-anchor="middle">Presidential Assent</text><path d="M 90 35 L 110 35 M 190 35 L 210 35" stroke="#000" stroke-width="1.5"/></svg>
Which essential parliamentary stage occurs immediately prior to the Committee Stage shown in this sequence?
qs.e: In legislative procedure, the Second Reading (where general principles of a bill are debated) occurs immediately before the bill is referred to the Committee Stage.

qs.q: The organ of the Commonwealth of Nations that convenes every two years to discuss global economic and political matters among member countries is
qs.e: CHOGM is the biennial summit bringing together leaders of Commonwealth nations to debate international issues and coordinate policy.

qs.q: Which military head of state promulgated Decree No. 34 of 1966 (the Unification Decree), attempting to abolish Nigeria's federal system?
qs.e: General Aguiyi-Ironsi promulgated Decree No. 34 in May 1966, unifying the civil service and abolishing regions, which provoked intense political resistance.

qs.q: A alien resident in Nigeria who fulfills a continuous legal residence requirement of 15 years, demonstrates good character, and takes an oath of allegiance can apply for citizenship by
qs.e: Under Section 27 of the 1999 Constitution, naturalization requires 15 years continuous residence, assimilation, good character, and an oath of allegiance.

qs.q: The Organization of Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC), which Nigeria joined in 1971, was originally founded to
o: Coordinate petroleum policies among member countries and stabilize global crude oil prices
Military enforce maritime blockade on non-member oil importers
Finance infrastructure developments in non-oil developing nations
Abolish commercial oil exploration in deep offshore territories
qs.e: OPEC was formed in 1960 to unify petroleum policies, secure fair oil prices for producer nations, and regulate production quotas.

qs.q: The military administration that created 12 states in Nigeria in May 1967 on the eve of the Civil War was headed by
qs.e: General Yakubu Gowon divided Nigeria's 4 regions into 12 states on May 27, 1967, replacing the regional arrangement with a multi-state federal structure.

qs.q: In political theory, the concept of Popular Sovereignty emphasizes that legitimate political power resides in the
o: Will of the people exercised through constitutional voting
Decisions rendered by international judicial bodies
Decrees issued by military supreme ruling councils
qs.e: Popular sovereignty asserts that all governmental power derives from the consent and sovereign authority of the citizens.

qs.q: A key feature of Feudalism as an economic and political system was that political authority was tied directly to
o: Industrial capital accumulation in urban factories
qs.e: Feudalism structured society around relationships derived from land holding in exchange for service or labor between lords and vassals.

qs.q: A major advantage of a written constitution over an unwritten constitution is that a written constitution
o: Is codified in a single clear document, making constitutional rights easier for citizens to know and enforce
Can be amended quickly without legislative debates
Grants absolute immunity to executive ministers against judicial trial
Eliminates the need for a supreme appellate court
qs.e: A written constitution consolidates fundamental laws in one accessible document, enhancing legal clarity and simplifying rights enforcement.

qs.q: The doctrine of judicial review empowers the judiciary to protect constitutional supremacy by
o: Striking down statutory enactments or executive acts that violate constitutional provisions
Drafting annual financial budgets for government executive departments
Conducting police investigations into political party finances
Appointing legislative committee members in parliament
qs.e: Judicial review allows courts to nullify any law or official act that conflicts with the constitution, maintaining constitutional supremacy.

qs.q: Under the 1999 Constitution of Nigeria, primary education, local health services, and rural road maintenance are executed as
o: Concurrent functions between state governments and local government councils
Exclusive responsibilities of the federal ministry of defense
Private corporate activities exempt from statutory oversight
Exclusive duties of international non-governmental bodies
qs.e: Under the Fourth Schedule, primary education and health services are participatory/concurrent duties where local councils collaborate with state governments.

qs.q: The 1960 Independence Constitution of Nigeria provided for a executive structure headed by a Prime Minister and a ceremonial Head of State represented by the
qs.e: Under the 1960 Independence Constitution, Queen Elizabeth II was ceremonial Head of State, represented locally by the Governor-General (Dr. Nnamdi Azikiwe).

qs.q: In the Nigerian Second Republic, which political party was founded by Alhaji Waziri Ibrahim under the banner of 'Politics Without Bitterness'?
qs.e: Waziri Ibrahim broke away from NPP to form the Great Nigeria People's Party (GNPP), campaigning under the slogan 'Politics Without Bitterness'.

qs.q: A sectional pressure group is distinguished from a cause pressure group because a sectional group
o: Represents and defends the specific social or economic interests of a defined section of society
Campaigns exclusively for global environmental protection issues
Is open to every citizen regardless of occupation or background
Refuses to participate in lobbying legislative committees
qs.e: Sectional groups (e.g., trade unions, professional associations) represent specific segments of society and defend their members' distinct material interests.

qs.q: Universal Adult Suffrage grants the right to vote in public elections to all adult citizens who meet statutory age requirements regardless of
o: Property ownership, gender, social status, or income
Educational qualifications and university degree holdings
Party registration fee payments to local councils
Military rank or civil service grade level
qs.e: Universal adult suffrage guarantees that all adult citizens meeting the age threshold can vote without property, wealth, gender, or social status restrictions.

qs.q: Loss of Nigerian citizenship by deprivation can apply to a naturalized citizen if the person is
o: Convicted of treason or sentenced to imprisonment for three years or more within seven years of naturalization
Elected as a local government ward councillor
Employed in a state civil service ministry
Registered as a member of a registered political party
qs.e: Under Section 30 of the 1999 Constitution, a naturalized citizen can be deprived of citizenship if convicted of treason or sentenced to prison for over 3 years within 7 years of naturalization.

qs.q: In the United Nations Security Council, the power of any of the five permanent members to block the adoption of a substantive resolution is known as the
qs.e: The veto power enables any permanent member (US, UK, France, Russia, China) to reject a substantive draft resolution regardless of majority support.

qs.q: The military regime of General Murtala Muhammed/General Olusegun Obasanjo (1975–1979) made a major historical contribution to Nigerian democracy by
o: Initiating and faithfully executing a structured transition programme that handed over power to an elected civilian government in 1979
Abolishing state governments and converting Nigeria into a permanent unitary state
Cancelling all local government statutory allocations from the central bank
Banning all trade unions and professional associations permanently
qs.e: The Murtala/Obasanjo regime drafted the 1979 Constitution, created 19 states, established local government reforms, and handed over power to Shehu Shagari on October 1, 1979.

qs.q: Comparing a unitary state with a federal state, a primary distinction is that in a unitary state
o: Sub-national regional authorities derive their powers from central government delegation rather than direct constitutional allotment
Regional units hold absolute sovereign authority to override central parliament
The judiciary is prohibited from hearing constitutional cases
Bicameralism is mandated across all sub-national municipal councils
qs.e: In a unitary state, sub-national divisions derive their existence and authority from central statutes, whereas in a federation, powers are constitutionally divided.

qs.q: The doctrine of separation of powers in a presidential democracy prevents tyranny primarily by ensuring that
o: No single branch of government concentrates total lawmaking, administrative, and judicial authority in its hands
The executive president can dismiss judges without legislative investigation
The legislature enacts laws without executive assent or veto
State governors command armed military units independently
qs.e: Separation of powers divides state functions among distinct organs so that no single organ holds unchecked or absolute government power.

qs.q: A Private Member's Bill in a parliamentary legislature is a proposed piece of legislation introduced by
o: An individual legislator who is not a government minister or executive official
The President or Cabinet minister on behalf of the executive branch
The Chief Justice of the Federation during judicial conference
A foreign diplomatic ambassador accredited to parliament
qs.e: A Private Member's Bill is introduced by an individual member of parliament in their capacity as a representative, rather than by a cabinet minister on behalf of the executive.

qs.q: In a parliamentary cabinet system, if a individual minister faces serious parliamentary criticism for departmental mismanagement, the convention of 'individual responsibility' mandates that
o: The individual minister takes personal blame and resigns from office
The entire cabinet automatically dissolves immediately
The supreme court nullifies the minister's personal assets
The permanent secretary assumes political leadership of parliament
qs.e: Individual ministerial responsibility holds that a minister is personally accountable to parliament for the actions and errors of their department.

qs.q: The Federal Character Commission (FCC) in Nigeria was established primarily to enforce constitutional compliance regarding
o: Equitable distribution of public service appointments and socio-economic infrastructure across all states
Registration of foreign diplomatic vehicles operating in state capitals
Collection of corporate income taxes from oil extraction firms
Conduct of primary school common entrance examinations
qs.e: The FCC is tasked with ensuring fair and equitable distribution of posts in federal public service and state institutions among all federating states.

qs.q: The 1988 Civil Service Reform in Nigeria altered the designation of Permanent Secretaries to Directors-General and made their appointments
o: Political appointments tied to the tenure of the appointing administration
Permanent career postings until mandatory retirement age
Decided through competitive examinations set by the United Nations
Subject to approval by traditional state chieftancy councils
qs.e: The 1988 reform re-designated Permanent Secretaries as Directors-General and made their tenure political, ending when the appointing administration left office (reversed by Ayida Panel in 1997).

qs.q: Under the 1999 Constitution of Nigeria, state creation requires a complex constitutional procedure including a two-thirds majority in the National Assembly, approval by state assemblies, and a successful
o: Referendum in the area requesting state creation supported by a two-thirds majority
Resolution passed by the Economic Community of West African States
Executive decree issued by the National Judicial Council
Unanimous vote by all local government chairmen in Nigeria
qs.e: Section 8 of the 1999 Constitution mandates a referendum supported by at least two-thirds of the population in the area requesting state creation, alongside legislative approvals.

qs.q: The primary objective of the Non-Aligned Movement (NAM), which Nigeria actively joined during the Cold War, was to
o: Maintain independence from Western and Eastern military blocs while supporting anti-colonial struggles
Form a unified military alliance with NATO forces in Western Europe
Establish a single global currency backed by crude oil reserves
Promote communist state revolutions across South America
qs.e: NAM was created during the Cold War so developing nations could avoid joining either the US-led Western or Soviet-led Eastern military alliances while upholding sovereign independence.

qs.q: The main problem encountered by the National Electoral Commission (NEC) in conducting the June 12, 1993 presidential election was
o: The political annulment of the election results by the Babangida military regime despite widespread peaceful voting
A total boycott of polling stations by all registered political voters
Widespread failure of electronic voting machines across state capitals
The refusal of foreign observers to monitor polling stations
qs.e: The June 12, 1993 presidential election (won by M.K.O. Abiola) was widely acclaimed as free and fair, but was arbitrarily annulled by General Babangida's military regime.

qs.q: An institutional pressure group operates within established institutions such as
o: The civil service, military, or state universities to influence administrative policy from within
Spontaneous street riot assemblies demanding immediate price controls
Foreign commercial embassies lobbying for tariff reductions
Religious pilgrimage boards managing overseas logistics
qs.e: Institutional pressure groups exist within formal governmental or social institutions (e.g. military officers, civil service staff associations) and exert internal policy influence.

qs.q: A Major feature of the 1989 Third Republic Constitution of Nigeria that differed from the 1979 Constitution was the mandatory statutory requirement for
o: A multi-party system with unlimited party registration
A zero-party system governed by traditional rulers
A single-party system headed by the military president
qs.e: The 1989 Constitution constitutionally restricted political party competition to exactly two government-created political parties (SDP and NRC).

qs.q: Public utilities such as water boards and electricity distribution firms are structured as public corporations primarily because
o: They provide essential services requiring high capital investment and state subsidy in the interest of social equity
They generate foreign currency reserves for state central banks
They are exempt from parliamentary budgetary oversight and state taxation
They operate exclusively under private international law
qs.e: Public utilities are managed as public corporations so state subsidies and regulations ensure affordable access to essential services for all citizens regardless of profit margins.

qs.q: Analyze the legal distinction between Citizenship by Birth and Citizenship by Registration under the 1999 Nigerian Constitution regarding Dual Citizenship. While a citizen by birth can hold dual citizenship freely, a person who acquires citizenship by registration
o: Must renounce their original foreign citizenship unless permitted under specific constitutional exceptions
Is automatically exempt from paying state income taxes
Gains immunity from criminal trial in Nigerian high courts
Cannot own moveable property in state capitals
qs.e: Section 28 specifies that citizens by registration or naturalization must renounce their previous foreign citizenship to hold Nigerian citizenship, unlike citizens by birth.

qs.q: Evaluate the transition of the Organization of African Unity (OAU) to the African Union (AU) under the Constitutive Act of 2000. A fundamental policy shift in the AU was
o: Adopting the right of intervention in member states in cases of war crimes, genocide, and unconstitutional changes of government
Abolishing all regional economic communities including ECOWAS and SADC
Prohibiting member states from holding seats in the United Nations Security Council
Enforcing a uniform continental military currency backed by mineral reserves
qs.e: Unlike the OAU's strict non-interference policy, Article 4(h) of the AU Constitutive Act empowers the AU to intervene in member states during gravity circumstances (genocide, war crimes, unconstitutional regime changes).

qs.q: Analyze the impact of military rule on Nigerian federalism between 1966 and 1999. Military governance altered federal operations primarily by
o: Centralizing political authority, administrative command, and fiscal revenue control through military command hierarchy
Expanding state legislative independence and regional police forces
Transferring supreme legislative powers to local government council chairmen
Abolishing the Supreme Court of Nigeria and state high courts
qs.e: Military regimes operated through hierarchical command, suspending regional autonomy and concentrating fiscal and legislative powers at the federal center.

qs.q: Under Section 12 of the 1999 Constitution of Nigeria, an international treaty signed by the Executive President becomes legally enforceable in domestic Nigerian courts only when
o: It is enacted into domestic law by an Act of the National Assembly
It is published in foreign diplomatic bulletins
It receives unanimous endorsement from state governors
It is ratified by the International Court of Justice
qs.e: Section 12(1) adopts a dualist approach: treaties signed by the President do not have force of law in Nigeria until enacted into domestic law by the National Assembly.

qs.q: The concept of Delegated Legislation is essential in modern public administration primarily because
o: Parliaments lack the technical expertise and legislative time to draft detailed administrative regulations for complex technical sectors
Executive ministers hold constitutional authority to override statutory acts
Judicial courts refuse to hear cases involving municipal regulations
State governors require delegated authority to command federal military garrisons
qs.e: Delegated legislation allows specialized administrative bodies to formulate technical, detailed rules efficiently, relieving parliament from drafting complex technical details.

qs.q: In administrative theory, the Udoji Public Service Review Commission of 1974 transformed Nigerian civil service administration by recommending
o: A unified grading and salary structure across the public sector and introduction of results-oriented management techniques
The abolition of all civil service pension schemes and retirement benefits
The merger of the civil service with political party administrative machinery
The privatization of all federal ministries and state secretariats
qs.e: The Udoji Commission introduced a Unified Grading and Salary Structure (UGSS) across the entire public service and championed modern management techniques like MBO (Management by Objectives).

qs.q: The primary objective of establishing the Public Complaints Commission (Ombudsman) in Nigeria in 1975 was to
o: Investigate administrative injustice, bureaucratic abuse, and unfair treatment of citizens by public officers
Enact statutory legislation for state legislative houses
Conduct criminal trials for election petition disputes
Regulate foreign currency exchange transactions in commercial banks
qs.e: The Public Complaints Commission (Ombudsman) provides citizens with accessible redress against bureaucratic oppression, administrative injustice, or abuse of office by public officials.

qs.q: A major argument against the Simple Majority / First-Past-The-Post electoral system in heterogeneous multi-ethnic societies is that it
o: Can produce legislative majorities for parties that receive less than 50% of the popular vote and exaggerate minority exclusion
Requires complex mathematical calculations that delay election results for months
Prevents political parties from fielding female legislative candidates
Forces all political parties into mandatory federal coalition governments
qs.e: First-Past-The-Post can result in 'wasted votes' and award disproportionate legislative majorities to a party winning pluralities, leaving substantial voting blocs unrepresented.

qs.q: The Willink Commission of 1958 was set up by the British colonial administration primarily to
o: Inquire into the fears of minority ethnic groups in Nigeria and propose means of allaying them
Draft the financial formula for regional crude oil derivation royalties
Conduct Nigeria's first universal adult suffrage national census
Establish the structure of the Federal Electoral Commission for the 1959 elections
qs.e: The 1958 Willink Commission investigated ethnic minority fears of domination by major ethnic groups in the three regions; it recommended inserting a Bill of Rights into the 1960 constitution.

qs.q: The main obstacle facing the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS) in achieving full economic integration is
o: Multiple currencies, trade barriers, political instability, and overlapping loyalties to francophone/anglophone blocs
Complete lack of natural resources among member states
Direct prohibition of intra-regional trade by the United Nations Charter
Military opposition from the African Union Peace and Security Council
qs.e: ECOWAS integration is hampered by currency diversity, tariff/non-tariff barriers, political instability/coups, and linguistic/colonial divisions (e.g. UMEAO vs Anglophone ties).

qs.q: Critique the role of ECOMOG in West African conflict management. While praised for restoring constitutional stability in Liberia and Sierra Leone, ECOMOG faced international legal scrutiny because its initial interventions
o: Were executed before receiving explicit formal prior authorization from the United Nations Security Council
Abolished all national borders among West African states permanent
Transferred gold mining rights directly to foreign private mercenaries
Prohibited civilian democratic elections after conflict cessation
qs.e: ECOMOG's emergency deployment in Liberia (1990) was initiated by West African leaders under ECOWAS before formal authorization by the UN Security Council, sparking legal debates on regional peace enforcement under Chapter VIII of the UN Charter.

qs.q: Analyze the constitutional contradiction inherent in military governance regarding the Rule of Law. Military regimes fundamentally undermine constitutionalism because they govern through
o: Military Decrees containing ouster clauses that explicitly exclude judicial review of executive actions
Parliamentary statutes passed by two-thirds supermajorities in elected assemblies
Binding judgments issued by international human rights courts
Referendums conducted among civil service labor unions
qs.e: Military Decrees often contain 'ouster clauses' barring courts from examining the constitutionality or validity of military executive actions, destroying judicial review and the rule of law.

qs.q: Compare the 1979 and 1999 Constitutions of Nigeria regarding local government financial autonomy. Despite declaring local councils as the third tier of government, both constitutions weakened local financial independence by
o: Mandating that federal statutory allocations be funneled through the State Joint Local Government Account managed by state governments
Prohibiting local government councils from receiving any share of federally collected revenue
Transferring local council revenue collection to the Federal Inland Revenue Service
Requiring local chairmen to pay all local tax revenues directly to traditional rulers
qs.e: The State Joint Local Government Account (Section 162(6)) enabled state governments to control and withhold statutory allocations meant for local councils, crippling local autonomy.

qs.q: Evaluate the political consequences of the 1953 Motion for Self-Government moved by Chief Anthony Enahoro in the House of Representatives. The motion triggered an acute constitutional crisis because it
o: Exposed deep North-South political rifts when Northern delegates substituted 'as soon as practicable' for '1956', leading to the walkout of Southern delegates
Resulted in the immediate military overthrow of the British colonial governor
Abolished the regional houses of assembly in the Western and Eastern regions
Forced Nigeria to secede immediately from the British Commonwealth of Nations
qs.e: Enahoro's 1956 self-government motion led to northern opposition (preferring 'as soon as practicable'), walkouts, insults in Lagos, and the Kano riots of 1953, accelerating regional breakdown and leading to the 1954 Lyttelton federal constitution.

qs.q: Assess the effectiveness of the Federal Civil Service Commission in insulating civil servants from political patronage. In practice, civil service neutrality is vulnerable to executive erosion because
o: The President appoints members of the Civil Service Commission subject to Senate confirmation, enabling political executive influence over key personnel decisions
Civil servants are constitutionally required to join the ruling political party upon promotion
Judicial courts possess statutory authority to write civil service promotion exams
State governors command the administrative postings of federal ministry clerks
qs.e: Because top appointments to the Civil Service Commission are made by the political executive (President/Governors), political considerations can influence appointments, tenure, and discipline.

qs.q: The core feature that distinguishes a state from other human associations or organizations is its monopoly over
o: Legitimate coercive physical force within its boundaries
qs.e: Max Weber famously defined the state as an institution holding a monopoly on the legitimate use of physical force within a given territory.

qs.q: An economic and social ideology advocating complete collective ownership, abolition of private enterprise, and a classless society is
qs.e: Communism is a far-left ideology that envisions a classless, stateless society based on common ownership of all means of production.

qs.q: The legal mechanism through which an act of parliament or executive decree is challenged in court for violating fundamental constitutional rights is called
qs.e: Judicial review enables courts to test the constitutionality of legislative and executive acts and strike down those that violate constitutional rights.

qs.q: Under a federal system of governance, matters placed on the Exclusive Legislative List are reserved solely for the
qs.e: Items on the Exclusive List are within the sole jurisdiction of the federal central parliament (e.g. National Assembly of Nigeria).

qs.q: The 1979 Constitution of Nigeria established a bicameral National Assembly consisting of the
o: House of Assembly and House of Chiefs
qs.e: The 1979 Constitution created a bicameral federal legislature comprising the Senate (upper house) and House of Representatives (lower house).

qs.q: An organized political organization whose chief goal is to win electoral contests and form the executive government is a
qs.e: A political party is an organized group of people with shared beliefs who field candidates in elections to gain public office and run government.

qs.q: The specialized administrative body established in Nigeria to manage the recruitment, promotion, and discipline of federal civil servants is the
qs.e: The Federal Civil Service Commission handles personnel management (recruitment, promotion, discipline) for federal civil service personnel.

qs.q: A citizen's obligation to pay statutory income taxes, defend the country against external aggression, and respect national symbols is classified as a
qs.e: Duties and obligations (such as tax payment, loyalty, and national defense) are constitutional expectations required of every patriotic citizen.

qs.q: The foreign policy doctrine of Non-Alignment adopted by many developing countries during the Cold War meant
o: Refusing to join formal military alliances with either the Western or Eastern superpower blocs
Abolishing all foreign trade treaties with industrialized nations
Establishing a single continental government under military leadership
Prohibiting citizens from traveling overseas for educational purposes
qs.e: Non-alignment meant maintaining independent diplomatic positioning without committing to either the US-led capitalist or Soviet-led communist military blocs.

qs.q: Which international financial institution provides long-term loans and grants to developing countries for infrastructure and capital projects?
qs.e: The World Bank (IBRD) provides financial and technical assistance to developing countries for capital projects like roads, power, and schools.

qs.q: Military governments in Nigeria routinely governed through federal instruments known as
qs.e: Federal military governments enact laws termed 'Decrees' (and state military governors issued 'Edicts'), which supersede ordinary constitutional provisions.

qs.q: A constitutional system where the head of state is an elected or appointed president rather than a hereditary monarch is a
qs.e: A republic is a state in which supreme power is held by the people and their elected representatives, with an elected president rather than a monarch.

qs.q: In a presidential system, the President's exercise of executive power is checked by the legislature through its power to
o: Confirm or reject presidential appointments of ministers, ambassadors, and judges
Issue judicial writs of habeas corpus directly against state governors
Dissolve the supreme court whenever legislative bills are invalidated
Appoint administrative heads of federal civil service directorates
qs.e: Legislative confirmation of executive appointments (ministers, ambassadors, judges) is a major constitutional check exercised by the legislature.

qs.q: The authority of a court to hear and determine a legal case in the first instance is known as its
qs.e: Original jurisdiction refers to a court's power to hear a case for the very first time, as distinguished from appellate jurisdiction.
