qs.e: Proverbs 15:1 provides practical interpersonal wisdom: 'A soft answer turneth away wrath: but grievous words stir up anger.'

qs.q: When Job experienced sudden loss of his children, wealth, and health, his initial faithful response was
o: 'I will offer sacrifices to foreign gods to regain my lost wealth'
'The LORD gave, and the LORD hath taken away; blessed be the name of the LORD'
'God has acted unrighteously by targeting an innocent believer'
'My wife was correct in advising me to curse God and die'
qs.e: Job 1:21 records Job's profound worship despite overwhelming sorrow: 'naked came I out of my mother's womb, and naked shall I return thither: the LORD gave, and the LORD hath taken away; blessed be the name of the LORD.'

qs.q: The central conclusion reached by the author of Ecclesiastes after examining all human pursuits under the sun is to
o: 'Withdraw completely from human society into solitary isolation'
'Pursue worldly fame and intellectual knowledge at all costs'
'Fear God, and keep his commandments: for this is the whole duty of man'
'Amass maximum silver and gold before physical strength fades'
qs.e: Ecclesiastes 12:13 concludes: 'Let us hear the conclusion of the whole matter: Fear God, and keep his commandments: for this is the whole duty of man.'

qs.q: The vision of the Valley of Dry Bones in Ezekiel 37 symbolized
o: the restoration and spiritual quickening of the hopeless, exiled house of Israel
the final destruction of Jerusalem by fire
the physical resurrection of all ancient pagan armies
the eternal punishment of the wicked in Sheol
qs.e: Ezekiel 37:11-14 explains that the dry bones represent the whole house of Israel in exile saying 'our hope is lost', whom God promises to revive and restore to their land.

qs.q: Daniel was thrown into the lions' den under King Darius because Daniel
o: stole silver vessels from the Babylonian royal palace
refused to interpret Darius' dream regarding the four kingdoms
refused to stop praying to the God of heaven three times a day despite a royal decree
encouraged the Persian army to launch a mutiny against Darius
qs.e: Daniel 6:10-16 records Daniel continuing his daily practice of praying toward Jerusalem, refusing to obey an unalterable decree that prohibited praying to any god except the king.

qs.q: Isaiah 7:14 contained the famous prophetic sign to King Ahaz declaring that
o: King Ahaz would live for fifteen additional years
Jerusalem would never fall to the Babylonian army
a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel
the Temple would be destroyed within forty days
qs.e: Isaiah 7:14 records the messianic sign: 'Behold, a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel' ('God with us').

qs.q: Micah 6:8 summarizes true religion and what the LORD requires of human beings as doing justly, loving mercy, and
o: building stone altars on every high hill
offering thousands of rams in sacrifice
qs.e: Micah 6:8 states: 'He hath showed thee, O man, what is good; and what doth the LORD require of thee, but to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God?'

qs.q: In Micah 5:2, the prophet foretold that the future Ruler and Shepherd of Israel would be born in
qs.e: Micah 5:2 explicitly names Bethlehem Ephrathah as the small town out of which Messiah would come forth whose goings forth have been from everlasting.

qs.q: The prophet Joel foretold a future day when God would pour out His Spirit upon all flesh (Joel 2:28), a prophecy quoted by Peter on the day of
qs.e: In Acts 2:16-21, Peter quotes Joel 2:28-32 to explain the Holy Spirit's miraculous outpouring upon the disciples in Jerusalem.

qs.q: When Satan tempted Jesus in the wilderness after His forty-day fast, Jesus repelled every temptation by
o: performing a dramatic miracle to blind the tempter
quoting written Scripture from the Old Testament Law ('It is written...')
calling down twelve legions of angels to defend Him
entering into a theological debate regarding his lineage
qs.e: In Matthew 4:1-11, Jesus refuted each of Satan's three temptations by citing Deuteronomy (Matt 4:4, 7, 10), demonstrating the authority and sufficiency of God's Word.

qs.q: Simeon's prophecy at Jesus' Temple presentation (Luke 2:25-35) declared that the infant Jesus was destined to be
o: a earthly military general who would expel the Romans
a wealthy king residing in the palace of Herod
a light to lighten the Gentiles, and the glory of God's people Israel
a high priest who would rebuild Solomon's Temple
qs.e: Luke 2:32 records Simeon's Nunc Dimittis, hailing Jesus as 'A light to lighten the Gentiles, and the glory of thy people Israel,' highlighting universal salvation.

qs.q: When Joseph discovered that Mary was pregnant before they came together, he initially decided to
o: take her immediately to Bethlehem without angelic guidance
demand a cash financial refund from Mary's family
divorce her quietly to avoid putting her to public shame, showing his righteous character
report her to the Sanhedrin for immediate execution by stoning
qs.e: Matthew 1:19 notes Joseph's compassion and righteousness: 'being a just man, and not willing to make her a publick example, was minded to put her away privily.'

qs.q: In Matthew 6:33, Jesus gave the core principle regarding anxiety and material needs by commanding believers to
o: 'Seek ye first the kingdom of God, and his righteousness; and all these things shall be added unto you'
'Store up massive financial reserves for future days of famine'
'Labor day and night without rest to secure physical food'
'Borrow money from neighbours whenever needs arise'
qs.e: Matthew 6:33 establishes priority: placing God's kingdom and righteousness first frees believers from anxiety, trusting God for daily material provision.

qs.q: The Golden Rule stated by Jesus in Matthew 7:12 instructs:
o: 'An eye for an eye, and a tooth for a tooth'
'Therefore all things whatsoever ye would that men should do to you, do ye even so to them'
'Love those who love you, and hate your enemies'
'Do unto others before they do unto you'
qs.e: Matthew 7:12 summarizes practical ethics: treating others with the same love, fairness, and kindness we desire for ourselves, fulfilling the Law and Prophets.

qs.q: Jesus warned against ostentatious hypocritical religious practices (almsgiving, prayer, and fasting in Matthew 6) by commanding that these acts be done
o: in the presence of church elders to verify spiritual sincerity
only during national annual feast holidays
on street corners to set a public example for unbelievers
in secret, so that the Father who sees in secret will reward open practice
qs.e: Matthew 6:1-18 rebukes religious showmanship meant to win human praise, instructing believers to give, pray, and fast secretly unto God.

qs.q: In the Parable of the Prodigal Son (Luke 15), when the younger son returned home broken and repentant, his father responded by
o: forcing him to work as a hired servant for seven years to repay his debt
running to embrace him, kissing him, and throwing a celebratory feast
demanding a public confession before the village elders
exiling him to the outer boundary of the village
qs.e: Luke 15:20-24 depicts the father's lavish grace: 'when he was yet a great way off, his father saw him, and had compassion, and ran, and fell on his neck, and kissed him.'

qs.q: The Parable of the Pharisee and the Tax Collector (Luke 18:9-14) teaches that God justifies those who pray with
o: detailed theological arguments concerning the Law
self-righteous boasting of good works and fasting
loud eloquent speeches in front of the altar
humble repentance ('God be merciful to me a sinner')
qs.e: Luke 18:13-14 shows the tax collector beating his breast in genuine humility, leaving justified, while the proud Pharisee was rejected.

qs.q: In the Parable of the Ten Virgins (Matthew 25), the five foolish virgins were unprepared for the bridegroom's arrival because they
o: took no extra oil in their vessels with their lamps
arrived at the banquet hall without money
fell asleep while waiting in the house
qs.e: Matthew 25:3 notes: 'They that were foolish took their lamps, and took no oil with them,' emphasizing spiritual vigilance and readiness for Christ's return.

qs.q: When Jesus calmed the raging storm on the Sea of Galilee (Mark 4:39), He commanded the wind and waves saying:
qs.e: Mark 4:39 records Jesus arising and rebuking the wind: 'Peace, be still. And the wind ceased, and there was a great calm,' demonstrating His authority over nature.

qs.q: Out of the ten lepers cleansed by Jesus in Luke 17:11-19, how many returned to glorify God and give Him thanks?
o: Five returned while five went to the priests
None returned because they were overwhelmed with joy
All ten returned in a solemn procession
Only one, who was a Samaritan
qs.e: Luke 17:15-16 records that only one cleansed leper—a Samaritan foreign outcast—returned, fell on his face at Jesus' feet, and gave thanks.

qs.q: When Jesus raised Lazarus from the dead in Bethany (John 11), Lazarus had been in the tomb for
qs.e: John 11:39 notes Martha's comment that Lazarus had been dead four days, making his resurrection an undeniable manifestation of divine power over physical death.

qs.q: In the courtyard of the High Priest during Jesus' trial, Peter denied knowing Jesus how many times before the cock crowed?
qs.e: Matthew 26:75 records Peter remembering Jesus' prediction: 'Before the cock crow, thou shalt deny me thrice,' weeping bitterly in repentance.

qs.q: At the moment of Jesus' death on the cross (Matthew 27:51), what miraculous event occurred inside the Jerusalem Temple?
o: The bronze laver overflowed with sacrificial water
The golden altar of incense collapsed into dust
The Ark of the Covenant vanished into heaven
The veil of the temple was rent in twain from the top to the bottom
qs.e: Matthew 27:51 records the tearing of the Temple veil, symbolizing direct access to God's presence opened for all believers through Christ's death (Hebrews 10:19-20).

qs.q: In the Great Commission (Matthew 28:18-20), Jesus commanded His resurrected disciples to go and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of
o: Moses, Elijah, and the Holy Prophets
the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost
the King of Kings and Lord of Lords
the Church of Jerusalem and the Apostles
qs.e: Matthew 28:19 specifies the Trinitarian baptismal formula given by Christ for disciple-making across all nations.

qs.q: The communal life of the early believers in Jerusalem recorded in Acts 2:42 was characterized by steadfast devotion to
o: exclusive dietary fasts without gathering together
the apostles' doctrine and fellowship, breaking of bread, and prayers
secular philosophical debates in public market places
qs.e: Acts 2:42 outlines the four foundational spiritual pillars of early church fellowship: apostolic doctrine, fellowship, communion, and prayer.

qs.q: Why were Ananias and Sapphira struck dead by God in Acts 5?
o: Because they opposed Peter's decision to preach to Gentiles
Because they lied to the Holy Spirit by deceptively holding back part of the land's sale price while pretending to give all
Because they refused to pay temple tax to the Jewish High Priest
Because they worshiped Roman idols in secret
qs.e: Acts 5:3-4 records Peter confronting Ananias: 'why hath Satan filled thine heart to lie to the Holy Ghost... thou hast not lied unto men, but unto God,' bringing solemn judgment for spiritual hypocrisy.

qs.q: In Acts 6, seven deacons including Stephen and Philip were appointed primarily to
o: guard the upper room against Temple guards
collect taxes for the Roman governor in Judea
replace the twelve apostles in preaching and doctrine
oversee the daily distribution of food to widows, resolving neglect between Hellenistic and Hebrew believers
qs.e: Acts 6:1-6 describes selecting seven men of honest report, full of the Holy Ghost and wisdom, to handle administrative food ministry so apostles could focus on prayer and word.

qs.q: Cornelius, who sent for Peter from Caesarea (Acts 10), was a Roman centurion described as
o: a harsh military tyrant who persecuted Christians
a priest of Zeus who practiced Roman astrology
a devout man who feared God, gave much alms, and prayed to God continually
a Jewish tax collector working for Herod
qs.e: Acts 10:1-2 introduces Cornelius as a God-fearing Gentile whose prayers and alms came up as a memorial before God.

qs.q: What vision did Peter receive on the rooftop in Joppa (Acts 10) to prepare him to visit Cornelius?
o: A burning bush that was not consumed by fire
A golden altar with fiery coals brought by seraphim
A ladder extending from heaven to earth with angels
A sheet let down from heaven containing all kinds of four-footed beasts, creeping things, and birds
qs.e: Acts 10:11-12 describes Peter's vision of the vessel like a great sheet, accompanied by a voice: 'What God hath cleansed, that call not thou common.'

qs.q: King Herod Agrippa I met a sudden, tragic death in Acts 12:21-23 because he
o: was defeated in battle by the King of Syria
fled to Rome after Peter's prison escape
accepted divine praise from the crowd without giving glory to God, and was eaten of worms
was poisoned by his own Roman palace guards
qs.e: Acts 12:22-23 records that when the people shouted 'It is the voice of a god, and not of a man', an angel smote Herod because he gave not God the glory.

qs.q: Philip preached the Gospel in the city of Samaria (Acts 8), where a famous sorcerer named Simon tried to
o: buy the power of imparting the Holy Spirit with money
report Philip to the Roman governor
stone Philip outside the city gates
challenge Philip to a magical duel
qs.e: Acts 8:18-19 records Simon Magus offering money to the apostles ('Give me also this power...'), originating the term 'simony' for buying spiritual offices.

qs.q: When Philip met the Ethiopian eunuch traveling in his chariot (Acts 8:26-39), the eunuch was reading from
o: Daniel 7, the vision of four beasts
Isaiah 53, the prophecy of the Suffering Servant
qs.e: Acts 8:32-35 identifies the text: Isaiah 53:7-8 ('He was led as a sheep to the slaughter...'), from which Philip preached unto him Jesus.

qs.q: What was Saul's role during the stoning of Stephen in Acts 7:58 & 8:1?
o: He held the coats of the witnesses and was consenting unto Stephen's death
He argued Stephen's legal defense before the High Priest
He attempted to stop the crowd from executing Stephen
He threw the first stone against Stephen
qs.e: Acts 7:58 & 8:1 state that the witnesses laid down their clothes at a young man's feet named Saul, and Saul was consenting unto his death.

qs.q: The fundamental reason God accepted Abel's offering but rejected Cain's was that
o: God prefers animal sacrifices over agricultural produce in all circumstances
Abel offered his sacrifice in faith and righteousness, whereas Cain's heart was wicked
Cain presented an offering that was physically smaller than Abel's
Abel was the older brother entitled to divine favor
qs.e: Hebrews 11:4 and Genesis 4:3-7 clarify that Abel offered by faith a more excellent sacrifice, whereas Cain's heart lacked faith and righteousness, leading to envy and anger.

qs.q: Comparing the creation narrative of Genesis 1 with that of Genesis 2 indicates that Genesis 2 emphasizes
o: the personal, relational connection between God, humanity, and the garden environment
the astronomical ordering of the physical cosmos over six solar days
the political boundaries of ancient Near Eastern kingdoms
the legal establishment of the Levitical sacrificial system
qs.e: Genesis 1 provides a broad cosmic overview of creation by God's word, while Genesis 2 focuses specifically on humanity's creation, environment, relationships, and moral responsibility.

qs.q: The mandate given to humanity in Genesis 1:28 to 'subdue' the earth and 'have dominion' implies
o: godly stewardship and responsible care over God's created world
the political subjugation of foreign nations by Israel
unrestricted exploitation of natural resources for selfish greed
the worship of natural elements as divine deities
qs.e: Dominion in Genesis 1:28 reflects God's delegating responsibility to humanity to act as righteous stewards over creation, caring for it in harmony with God's character.

qs.q: Melchizedek, who met Abraham after the defeat of the eastern kings, held the dual title of
o: Captain of the Host and Judge of Hebron
King of Sodom and Prophet of Yahweh
High Priest of Bethel and Ruler of Canaan
King of Salem and Priest of the Most High God
qs.e: Genesis 14:18 identifies Melchizedek as King of Salem and the priest of the most high God, who brought out bread and wine and blessed Abram.

qs.q: Jacob's dream at Bethel featuring a ladder reaching to heaven revealed to him that
o: he must immediately return to his father Isaac's house
Esau was actively pursuing him with four hundred armed men
he was destined to conquer Egypt with a great military army
God's presence and covenant promise accompanied him even in exile away from home
qs.e: In Genesis 28:12-15, God reaffirmed the Abrahamic covenant to Jacob at Bethel, assuring him 'I am with thee, and will keep thee in all places whither thou goest.'

qs.q: The name change from Jacob to Israel at Peniel marked a transformation in Jacob's life because it signified that
o: he was now the political ruler over all Twelve Tribes
he had striven with God and men and had prevailed, abandoning his deceitful reliance on self
God had exempted his family from all future earthly trials
his brother Esau had officially surrendered the patriarchate to him
qs.e: Genesis 32:28 records: 'Thy name shall be called no more Jacob, but Israel: for as a prince hast thou power with God and with men, and hast prevailed.'

qs.q: When Joseph planted his silver cup in Benjamin's sack, his main objective was to test whether his brothers
o: had truly repented and would protect Benjamin rather than abandon him as they did Joseph
knew Joseph's true identity without him revealing it
were carrying hidden Egyptian gold back to Canaan
intended to launch a rebellion against Pharaoh's palace
qs.e: Genesis 44 shows Joseph testing his brothers' character to see if they would sacrifice themselves for Benjamin, which Judah demonstrated by offering to stay as a slave.

qs.q: Judah's willingness to stay as a slave in Egypt in place of Benjamin (Genesis 44:33) demonstrated that Judah
o: feared being executed immediately by the Egyptian guards
wished to live permanently in Egypt rather than return to Canaan
was secretly conspiring with Pharaoh's officials against Jacob
had undergone a genuine transformation from self-interest to sacrificial love for his family
qs.e: In Genesis 44:33, Judah's self-sacrificial offer to take Benjamin's place proved a profound moral change from when he suggested selling Joseph in Genesis 37:26.

qs.q: Joseph's statement to his brothers in Genesis 50:20 ('As for you, ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good') highlights the principle of divine
o: arbitrary fate overriding all human choices
providential sovereignty using human actions to accomplish salvation
unconditional election of foreign monarchs over Israel
retributive justice destroying evil nations instantly
qs.e: Genesis 50:20 illustrates providence: God overrules human evil and malice to bring about His good purpose, preserving life during severe famine.

qs.q: The First Commandment ('Thou shalt have no other gods before me') differs from the Second Commandment in that the Second Commandment specifically forbids
o: taking the name of Yahweh in vain through false oaths
working on the holy Sabbath day of rest
coveting a neighbor's house or livestock
making and worshipping carved images or idols of any kind
qs.e: Exodus 20:3-5 distinguishes exclusive worship of Yahweh (1st Commandment) from prohibition against making graven images to represent or worship God (2nd Commandment).

qs.q: During the Golden Calf incident (Exodus 32), Moses' intercession on Mount Sinai appealed fundamentally to
o: Israel's flawless track record of obedience since leaving Egypt
Aaron's innocent lack of awareness during idol construction
the economic wealth Israel brought out of Egypt
God's covenant promise to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob and God's honor among the nations
qs.e: In Exodus 32:11-13, Moses pleaded for mercy based on God's reputation before Egypt and His immutable covenant promises to the patriarchs.

qs.q: The ten plagues inflicted upon Egypt were spiritually designed by Yahweh primarily to
o: demonstrate His absolute supremacy over the pantheon of Egyptian gods
destroy the entire agricultural infrastructure of the Nile delta permanently
test Israel's military readiness for conquering Canaan
force Pharaoh to pay financial wages to Hebrew laborers
qs.e: Exodus 12:12 states: 'against all the gods of Egypt I will execute judgment: I am the LORD,' exposing the impotence of Egyptian deities.

qs.q: Gideon was nicknamed 'Jerubbaal' after he took a courageous stand by
o: refusing to accept the crown when Israel offered to make him king
sacrificing a bull on Mount Carmel
killing the king of Midian with a golden spear
tearing down his father's altar of Baal and cutting down the wooden Asherah pole
qs.e: Judges 6:31-32 records that Joash named Gideon 'Jerubbaal' (meaning 'Let Baal plead against him') after Gideon destroyed Baal's altar.

qs.q: The tragedy of Jephthah's rash vow (Judges 11) illustrates the severe danger of
o: making foolish, unguided promises to God without scriptural discernment
refusing to fight against foreign oppressors
accepting leadership over an outlaw group in Gilead
qs.e: Jephthah's vow to offer whatever came out of his house first resulted in tragic consequences for his only daughter, warning against rash, unscriptural vows (Judges 11:30-39).

qs.q: Boaz acted as a 'kinsman-redeemer' (Goel) for Ruth and Naomi by fulfilling his legal obligation to
o: consecrate Ruth as a priestess in the tabernacle at Shiloh
pay Naomi's debts to the Moabite government
redeem Elimelech's land inheritance and marry Ruth to perpetuate the deceased family name
build a city of refuge in the territory of Judah
qs.e: Ruth 4:9-10 details Boaz fulfilling the duty of the kinsman-redeemer under Levitical law (Lev 25, Deut 25), buying Naomi's land and marrying Ruth.

qs.q: David refused to kill Saul when he had the opportunity in the cave at En-gedi because
o: the prophet Gad commanded David to make peace with Saul
Saul's armor bearer was standing guard at the cave entrance
Saul was the LORD's anointed, and David trusted God to execute judgment in His time
David feared Saul's army would immediately execute Jonathan
qs.e: 1 Samuel 24:6 shows David's reverence for God's anointed king: 'The LORD forbid that I should do this thing unto my master, the LORD's anointed.'

qs.q: In the Davidic Covenant (2 Samuel 7), God promised David that
o: the capital city would be moved from Jerusalem to Hebron
his descendants would never suffer military defeat or political trial
the Temple would be built during David's personal lifetime
His royal throne and throne of his kingdom would be established forever
qs.e: 2 Samuel 7:12-16 contains God's covenant promise to David that his kingdom and throne would be established unconditionally for eternity, fulfilled ultimately in Christ.

qs.q: Nathan the prophet confronted King David regarding his sin with Bathsheba and Uriah by telling a parable about
o: a vineyard owner whose tenants killed his messengers
a king who invited ungrateful guests to a wedding feast
a rich man who seized a poor man's single beloved ewe lamb
two brothers arguing over their father's cattle inheritance
qs.e: 2 Samuel 12:1-7 records Nathan telling the parable of the rich man and the ewe lamb, driving home David's guilt with 'Thou art the man!'

qs.q: Jezebel engineered the judicial murder of Naboth by arranging for false witnesses to accuse him of
o: conspiring with the Syrian army against Samaria
stealing gold from the royal palace treasury
offering unholy fire upon the high places
blaspheming God and cursing the king
qs.e: 1 Kings 21:10 explains Jezebel's plot: setting two 'sons of Belial' to testify that Naboth did blaspheme God and the king, leading to his stoning.

qs.q: The phrase 'the sin of Jeroboam son of Nebat' repeated throughout 1 & 2 Kings refers to
o: instituting unauthorized, idolatrous worship centers that led the entire northern kingdom into apostasy
taxing the Levites living in the northern territory
refusing to build stone fortifications around Samaria
marrying pagan wives from Ammon and Moab
qs.e: Jeroboam's golden calves at Dan and Bethel established state-sponsored idolatry, serving as the benchmark of covenant unfaithfulness for all subsequent northern kings.

qs.q: The unnamed man of God from Judah who prophesied against Jeroboam's altar at Bethel (1 Kings 13) was killed by a lion because he
o: accepted money from Jeroboam to reverse his prophetic curse
worshipped the golden calf at Bethel before leaving
disobeyed God's direct command by eating bread and drinking water in Bethel after being deceived by an old prophet
fled to Egypt instead of returning directly to Judah
qs.e: 1 Kings 13:18-24 illustrates that divine commands require unyielding obedience; believing a lying prophet did not excuse disobeying God's explicit word.

qs.q: When Elijah fled to Mount Horeb in fear of Jezebel (1 Kings 19), God revealed His presence to him not in the strong wind, earthquake, or fire, but in
o: a still small voice (a gentle whisper)
qs.e: 1 Kings 19:11-12 records God revealing Himself in 'a still small voice,' teaching Elijah that God works through quiet, persistent spiritual renewal.

qs.q: The miracle of Elisha making the iron axe head float (2 Kings 6) demonstrates God's concern for
o: the practical everyday needs and distresses of His humble servants
proving Elisha's superiority over secular blacksmiths
the military technology of Israel's army
building physical structures without human labor
qs.e: 2 Kings 6:1-7 records Elisha recovering a borrowed axe head for a poor member of the sons of the prophets, illustrating divine care over practical daily affairs.

qs.q: Elisha's promise of abundant food to famished Samaria during the Syrian siege was fulfilled when four leprous men discovered that
o: the king of Egypt had sent secret grain supply convoys
the citizens of Samaria had breached the Syrian camp
rain had fallen and produced an instantaneous wheat harvest
the Syrian army had panicked and fled, leaving behind all their provisions and tents
qs.e: 2 Kings 7:3-8 describes four lepers entering the Syrian camp to find it abandoned by divine intervention, fulfilling Elisha's prophecy of cheap food within 24 hours.

qs.q: King Josiah initiated a sweeping religious reform in Judah (2 Kings 22-23) after
o: Jeremiah was released from the muddy dungeon cistern
Hilkiah the high priest discovered the Book of the Law in the Temple during repairs
the Babylonian army lifted its first siege of Jerusalem
an angel of the Lord struck down 185,000 Assyrian soldiers
qs.e: 2 Kings 22:8-13 describes the discovery of the Law in the Temple, which moved young King Josiah to tear his clothes in repentance and cleanse the land of idols.

qs.q: When Sanballat and Tobiah mocked and threatened the rebuilding of Jerusalem's walls, Nehemiah responded by
o: challenging Sanballat to a sword duel outside the city
combining persistent prayer with practical defense, arming workers while they built
offering financial bribes to Sanballat to secure peace
halting construction until the Persian king sent additional troops
qs.e: Nehemiah 4:9, 17 records: 'Nevertheless we made our prayer unto our God, and set a watch against them day and night... every one with one of his hands wrought in the work, and with the other hand held a weapon.'

qs.q: Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego chose to be thrown into the burning fiery furnace rather than
o: bow down and worship King Nebuchadnezzar's golden image
pay annual tribute tax to the Babylonian treasury
stop praying toward Jerusalem three times a day
eat food from the king's royal banquet table
qs.e: Daniel 3:16-18 records their resolute faith: 'our God whom we serve is able to deliver us... But if not, be it known unto thee, O king, that we will not serve thy gods.'

qs.q: The primary flaw in the arguments of Job's three friends (Eliphaz, Bildad, and Zophar) was their rigid assumption that
o: all intense suffering is a direct, mechanical punishment for specific secret sins
Satan possesses equal authority and power to Almighty God
God is indifferent to human suffering and justice
Job was a foreign pagan who had never known Yahweh
qs.e: Job's friends applied a simplistic, mechanical retributive theology, insisting Job must have committed hidden sins to deserve such suffering, which God refuted in Job 42:7.

qs.q: When God finally spoke to Job out of the whirlwind (Job 38-41), God helped Job understand that
o: earthly suffering is purely accidental and outside divine oversight
Job's suffering was caused by his failure to offer morning burnt offerings
human beings cannot fathom God's infinite wisdom and cosmic governance, requiring trust rather than demands for explanation
Job's three friends were wiser theologians than Job himself
qs.e: God answered Job by pointing to His majestic creation (Job 38-41), demonstrating that human knowledge is finite, and trusting God's sovereign goodness is ultimate wisdom.

qs.q: Proverbs 6 commends the sluggard (lazy person) to observe and learn diligence from
o: the ant, which provides her meat in the summer without a ruler or overseer
the ox, which knows its master's crib
the eagle, which flies high in the heavens
the lion, which is strongest among beasts
qs.e: Proverbs 6:6-8 advises: 'Go to the ant, thou sluggard; consider her ways, and be wise: Which having no guide, overseer, or ruler, Provideth her meat in the summer...'

qs.q: Jeremiah's Temple Sermon in Jeremiah 7 warned the people of Judah against
o: placing superstitious trust in the physical Temple while continuing in social injustice and idolatry
offering sacrifices without paying the required temple tax
allowing Gentile converts to enter the inner courtyard
singing psalms without harp musical accompaniment
qs.e: Jeremiah 7:4-7 rebuked Judah for chanting 'The temple of the LORD', warning that physical religious institutions would not save them from judgment if they practiced injustice and idolatry.

qs.q: In Ezekiel 3 and 33, God designated Ezekiel as a 'watchman' unto the house of Israel, meaning he was responsible to
o: collect tithes and offerings for the exiled Levites
record the chronological reigns of foreign monarchs
faithfully warn the wicked and righteous of judgment, bearing personal accountability for delivering the message
guard the city gates against physical Babylonian spies
qs.e: Ezekiel 3:17-19 explains the watchman duty: if the prophet fails to warn the wicked, their blood is required at his hand; if he warns them, he delivers his own soul.

qs.q: Isaiah 53 describes the Suffering Servant who was 'wounded for our transgressions, bruised for our iniquities', pointing to
o: the martyrdom of the prophet Jeremiah in Egypt
substitutionary atonement accomplished through Christ's suffering and sacrifice
the military humiliation of King Hezekiah by Assyria
the physical defeat of King Nebuchadnezzar by Cyrus
qs.e: Isaiah 53 provides a profound messianic prophecy of the Servant taking upon Himself the sins and punishment of humanity to bring peace and healing.

qs.q: The primary theme of the prophet Amos' preaching was a passionate demand for
o: social justice, righteous treatment of the poor, and moral integrity over empty religious rituals
rebuilding the physical walls of Jerusalem
engaging in holy war against the Edomites
establishing an elite school of prophets at Gilgal
qs.e: Amos 5:24 encapsulates Amos' core message: 'But let judgment run down as waters, and righteousness as a mighty stream,' condemning hypocritical feasts while oppressing the needy.

qs.q: Jonah's initial reluctance to preach to Nineveh stemmed fundamentally from his
o: fear that the Ninevites would physically torture and execute him
desire to remain in Jerusalem as a temple singer
inability to speak the Assyrian language fluently
knowledge that God was merciful and gracious, and Jonah did not want Israel's cruel enemy spared
qs.e: Jonah 4:2 reveals Jonah's motive: he fled to Tarshish because he knew God was gracious and merciful, and he harbored nationalist resentment against Assyria.

qs.q: Habakkuk 2:4 contains the profound theological declaration that 'the just shall live by his...'
o: works; keeping ceremonial purity laws strictly
sword; defending the borders against foreign armies
wealth; amassing reserves for national famines
faith; trusting God's sovereign justice even when evil seems to prevail
qs.e: Habakkuk 2:4 states 'the just shall live by his faith,' a foundational text picked up in Romans 1:17, Galatians 3:11, and Hebrews 10:38.

qs.q: John the Baptist rebuked the Pharisees and Sadducees coming to his baptism by warning them not to rely on
o: their wealth gathered from Roman tax farming
their military alliances with the Edomite rulers
their physical lineage as children of Abraham, demanding fruits meet for repentance
their ability to recite the Psalms from memory
qs.e: Matthew 3:8-9 records John preaching: 'Bring forth therefore fruits meet for repentance: And think not to say within yourselves, We have Abraham to our father...'

qs.q: The visit of the Gentile Magi (Wise Men) from the East bringing gifts of gold, frankincense, and myrrh (Matthew 2) signifies
o: the financial funding required to buy land in Nazareth
the establishment of a trade route between Jerusalem and Persia
the political submission of Babylon to King Herod
the recognition and worship of Jesus as King, God, and Savior by the Gentile nations
qs.e: Matthew 2:1-12 reveals Gentile rulers worshipping the young Messiah with royal gifts, fulfilling Old Testament prophecies of Gentile inclusion (Isaiah 60:6).

qs.q: When twelve-year-old Jesus was found by His parents in the Jerusalem Temple (Luke 2:49), His statement 'Wist ye not that I must be about my Father's business?' demonstrated His early awareness of
o: His desire to become a licensed Rabbinical lawyer in Judah
His unique divine Sonship and singular commitment to His heavenly Father's mission
His dissatisfaction with Joseph's carpentry trade
His plan to join the Zealot political resistance movement
qs.e: Luke 2:49 records Jesus' first recorded words, revealing His distinct divine consciousness and priority of His Father's spiritual work over earthly familial ties.

qs.q: How did Jesus deepen the sixth commandment ('Thou shalt not kill') in Matthew 5:21-22?
o: He restricted the commandment exclusively to the High Priest
He taught that unrighteous anger and contemptuous speech against a brother make one guilty of judgment
He stated that physical murder is acceptable during times of national war
He abolished the commandment and replaced it with civil law
qs.e: Matthew 5:21-22 shows Jesus expanding murder from outward execution to root heart attitudes of anger, malice, and insulting words ('Raca').

qs.q: In the Parable of the Two Builders (Matthew 7:24-27), the wise man who built his house upon the rock represents anyone who
o: memorizes the Mosaic Law without acting upon it
builds elaborate physical church buildings in cities
fasts twice a week and tithes all possessions
hears Jesus' words and puts them into daily practice
qs.e: Matthew 7:24 states: 'whosoever heareth these sayings of mine, and doeth them, I will liken him unto a wise man, which built his house upon a rock.'

qs.q: When Jesus commanded 'Judge not, that ye be not judged' in Matthew 7:1-5, He instructed believers to first
o: cast out the beam from their own eye before attempting to remove the mote from a brother's eye
condemn unbelievers while ignoring internal church fellowship
report all moral offenses to civil magistrates immediately
assume that all human behavior is morally equivalent
qs.e: Matthew 7:1-5 warns against hypocritical, hyper-critical judgment, urging deep self-examination and repentance before attempting to correct others.

qs.q: The main lesson of the Parable of the Unforgiving Servant (Matthew 18:21-35) is that believers must forgive others because
o: forgiving others earns financial prosperity on earth
the Mosaic Law requires forgiving offenders exactly seven times
God has forgiven them an unpayable debt of sin, making unforgiveness toward others a contradiction of grace
failure to forgive results in public trial by secular courts
qs.e: Matthew 18:32-35 illustrates that receiving God's immense mercy obligates believers to extend heart-felt forgiveness to fellow humans.

qs.q: In the Parable of the Rich Fool (Luke 12:13-21), God called the wealthy farmer a 'fool' because he
o: hoarded material wealth for selfish ease while being spiritually bankrupt toward God
refused to hire workers during the grain harvest
invested his wealth in foreign Roman commerce
stole land from poor neighboring farmers in Israel
qs.e: Luke 12:20-21 warns: 'Thou fool, this night thy soul shall be required of thee... So is he that layeth up treasure for himself, and is not rich toward God.'

qs.q: The Parable of the Wheat and Tares (Matthew 13:24-30) explains that the righteous and the wicked will co-exist in the world until
o: a national catastrophe destroys physical agriculture
the final harvest at the end of the age, when angels will separate them for judgment
the Roman empire converts to Christianity
the church executes all false teachers
qs.e: Matthew 13:38-40 clarifies that the field is the world, and reapers are angels who will separate the righteous from the wicked at the end of the age.

qs.q: When four men lowered a paralytic man through the roof before Jesus (Mark 2:1-12), Jesus first declared to the sick man:
o: 'Arise, take up thy bed and run home'
'Thy faith has made thee a Roman citizen'
qs.e: Mark 2:5 shows Jesus addressing spiritual need first: 'Son, thy sins be forgiven thee,' provoking Pharisees and proving His authority to forgive sins.

qs.q: The Roman centurion whose servant was sick in Capernaum (Matthew 8:5-13) demonstrated extraordinary faith by asserting that
o: Jesus only needed to speak the word from a distance, and his servant would be healed
he would build a new synagogue in exchange for the miracle
Jesus must physically touch his servant in his house
his servant was worthy because of Roman military power
qs.e: Matthew 8:8-10 records the centurion recognizing Jesus' supreme authority: 'speak the word only, and my servant shall be healed,' marveling Jesus.

qs.q: The woman with the issue of blood for twelve years was healed instantly when she (Mark 5:25-34)
o: washed her face in the pool of Siloam
touched the hem of Jesus' garment in active faith
asked the apostles to lay hands upon her head
offered a financial sacrifice at the Jerusalem Temple
qs.e: Mark 5:28-29 describes her personal faith: 'If I may touch but his clothes, I shall be whole,' drawing healing power immediately from Jesus.

qs.q: When Pilate offered to release a prisoner according to Passover custom, the crowd demanded the release of Barabbas instead of Jesus because
o: Pilate forced the Jewish crowd to select a convicted murderer
the chief priests and elders persuaded the multitude to ask for Barabbas and destroy Jesus
Jesus requested that Barabbas be released in His place
Barabbas was a peaceful religious scholar loved by the poor
qs.e: Matthew 27:20 notes: 'But the chief priests and elders persuaded the multitude that they should ask Barabbas, and destroy Jesus,' choosing an insurrectionist murderer over the sinless Savior.

qs.q: Jesus' cry from the cross 'Eli, Eli, lama sabachthani?' ('My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?') in Matthew 27:46 is a direct quotation of
o: Genesis 3:15, declaring victory over the serpent
Psalm 22:1, expressing the intense spiritual reality of bearing human sin
qs.e: Matthew 27:46 quotes Psalm 22:1, fulfilling messianic prophecy as Jesus endured judicial separation while bearing human guilt.

qs.q: When Thomas doubted the resurrection of Jesus (John 20:24-29), asserting he would not believe unless he saw the nail prints, Jesus responded by showing his wounds and declaring:
o: 'Signs are reserved only for Gentiles and tax collectors'
'Go into the wilderness and fast seven days'
'Thy unbelief has excluded thee from the apostolate'
'Blessed are they that have not seen, and yet have believed'
qs.e: John 20:29 records Jesus gentle rebuke and blessing upon future generations who walk by faith: 'blessed are they that have not seen, and yet have believed.'

qs.q: When Peter and John healed the lame man at the Beautiful Gate (Acts 3:6), Peter declared:
o: 'Pay a vow at the altar of the sanctuary'
'Silver and gold have I none; but such as I have give I thee: In the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth rise up and walk'
'By my own holiness and power I make thee whole'
'Go wash in the pool of Siloam seven times'
qs.e: Acts 3:6 records Peter deflecting self-glory, performing the miracle strictly through faith in the authority and name of Jesus Christ.

qs.q: When the Sanhedrin commanded Peter and John to stop speaking or teaching in the name of Jesus (Acts 4:19-20), they responded:
o: 'We will move our ministry permanently to Samaria'
'Whether it be right in the sight of God to hearken unto you more than unto God, judge ye. For we cannot but speak the things which we have seen and heard'
'We will appeal directly to the Roman Emperor Caesar'
'We will obey your command provided you grant us money'
qs.e: Acts 4:19-20 expresses holy courage: obeying divine authority above human prohibition when civil/religious mandates contradict God's commands.

qs.q: The wise Pharisee Gamaliel advised the Sanhedrin regarding the apostles (Acts 5:38-39) that
o: the apostles should be banished to the island of Patmos
the Roman soldiers should be ordered to destroy the church
if this counsel or work be of men, it will come to nought; but if it be of God, ye cannot overthrow it
the apostles should be executed immediately by stoning
qs.e: Acts 5:38-39 records Gamaliel's prudent counsel: urging restraint lest the Sanhedrin be found fighting against God Himself.

qs.q: The fundamental theological lesson Peter learned from his vision and encounter with Cornelius was that
o: Gentiles must convert to Judaism before believing in Christ
Jewish Christians must not associate with non-Jews under any circumstance
'God is no respecter of persons: But in every nation he that feareth him, and worketh righteousness, is accepted with him'
Roman soldiers are exempt from baptism and repentance
qs.e: Acts 10:34-35 records Peter's breakthrough realization that God shows no racial or national partiality in offering salvation through Christ.

qs.q: When Peter returned to Jerusalem after baptizing Cornelius (Acts 11), the circumcised Jewish believers initially criticized him for
o: going in to uncircumcised men and eating with them
failing to consult the High Priest before leaving Joppa
accepting monetary gifts from a Roman officer
qs.e: Acts 11:2-3 notes that legalistic Jewish believers contended with Peter for breaking ceremonial social distance rules by eating with Gentile converts.

qs.q: The outpouring of the Holy Spirit upon Cornelius' household while Peter was still speaking (Acts 10:44-48) proved to Peter and his companions that
o: tongues of fire are required for every civil officer
the Jerusalem church should move its headquarters to Caesarea
Cornelius was destined to replace Judas Iscariot as an apostle
God had granted Gentiles repentance unto life without requiring Mosaic circumcision first
qs.e: Acts 10:45-47 records the Jewish believers being astonished because the gift of the Holy Spirit was poured out on Gentiles, validating their immediate water baptism.

qs.q: In his speech before the Sanhedrin (Acts 7), Stephen summarized Israel's national history to prove that Israel had consistently
o: kept the Mosaic Law with complete moral perfection
built holy sanctuaries in accordance with divine instructions
resisted the Holy Spirit and rejected God's appointed messengers, just as their fathers did
welcomed foreign prophets into their cities
qs.e: Acts 7:51 encapsulates Stephen's indictment: 'Ye stiffnecked and uncircumcised in heart and ears, ye do always resist the Holy Ghost: as your fathers did, so do ye.'

qs.q: How did Peter severely rebuke Simon the Sorcerer when Simon attempted to buy spiritual authority (Acts 8:20-22)?
o: 'Thy money perish with thee, because thou hast thought that the gift of God may be purchased with money'
'Pay your money directly to the widows in Jerusalem'
'Go into the desert and fast for forty days'
'You are appointed deacon over the Samaritan church'
qs.e: Acts 8:20 contains Peter's stern condemnation of commercializing spiritual gifts and grace, calling Simon to repent of his wicked heart.

qs.q: Just before his execution, Stephen looked up steadfastly into heaven (Acts 7:55-56) and saw
o: a sheet descending containing clean and unclean animals
the glory of God, and Jesus standing on the right hand of God
a golden temple surrounded by twelve thrones
qs.e: Acts 7:55-56 records Stephen's heavenly vision of Jesus standing at God's right hand, ready to receive His faithful witness.

qs.q: How were Paul and Silas delivered from the Philippian prison in Acts 16:25-31 after singing praises to God at midnight?
o: An angel struck the prison guards blind
Roman soldiers arrived with a pardon signed by Caesar
The Philippian jailer unlocked their chains secretly
A great earthquake shook the foundations, opening all prison doors and loosening their bands
qs.e: Acts 16:25-26 describes the miraculous midnight earthquake that unloosed prison bands, leading to the conversion of the Philippian jailer and his household.

qs.q: At the Areopagus in Athens (Acts 17:22-31), Paul used an inscription he saw in their city to preach the true Creator God. What was that inscription?
qs.e: Acts 17:23 records Paul skillfully connecting with Greek thinkers via their altar 'TO THE UNKNOWN GOD', proclaiming the ONE God who made the world and raised Jesus from the dead.

qs.q: In Ephesus (Acts 19), Demetrius the silversmith sparked a major riot against Paul because Paul's preaching threatened
o: their lucrative trade of making silver shrines for the goddess Artemis (Diana)
the physical safety of the Jewish synagogue elders
the trade routes between Ephesus and Jerusalem
the taxation revenue of the Roman governor Felix
qs.e: Acts 19:24-27 records Demetrius stirring up fellow craftsmen because Paul taught that gods made with human hands are no gods, undermining the cult of Artemis.

qs.q: In Galatians 3:24, Paul describes the Mosaic Law as a 'schoolmaster' (tutor) designed to
o: bring us unto Christ, that we might be justified by faith
condemn Gentiles while exalting physical Jews
provide permanent, eternal salvation apart from Christ
replace Abraham's covenant of promise permanently
qs.e: Galatians 3:24 explains the Law's temporary pedagogical purpose: exposing sin and driving sinners to Christ for justification by faith.

qs.q: In Philippians 2:5-11 (the Christ Hymn), Paul highlights Christ's incarnation and humility (kenosis) by emphasizing that He
o: demanded earthly royal service from Roman authorities
made Himself of no reputation, took upon Him the form of a servant, and humbled Himself unto death on the cross
retained His visible heavenly glory while walking on earth
refused to experience real human temptation or suffering
qs.e: Philippians 2:5-8 models supreme humility: Christ setting aside divine privileges to take servant form and endure cross death, resulting in exaltation.

qs.q: In Ephesians 6:10-18, Paul instructs believers to put on the 'whole armour of God' because Christian warfare is not against flesh and blood, but against
o: principalities, powers, rulers of darkness of this world, and spiritual wickedness in high places
secular Roman governors and tax collectors
qs.e: Ephesians 6:12 identifies the true nature of Christian struggle: supernatural spiritual warfare requiring divine defensive and offensive armor.

qs.q: In 1 Peter 2:9, believers are described as 'a chosen generation, a royal priesthood, an holy nation, a peculiar people' whose purpose is to
o: shew forth the praises of him who hath called you out of darkness into his marvellous light
impose Jewish dietary regulations upon all nations
rule over earthly secular governments by political force
rebuild the physical Temple in Jerusalem
qs.e: 1 Peter 2:9 defines church identity and mission: a consecrated royal priesthood called to proclaim God's praises and virtues to the world.

qs.q: In 1 Timothy 3:1-7, qualifications for a bishop (overseer) in the church require that he be blameless, the husband of one wife, vigilant, sober, and
o: a recent convert possessing great financial wealth
a trained Roman lawyer skilled in civil litigation
apt to teach, ruling well his own house, and having a good report of them which are without
a celibate ascetic living in solitary desert isolation
qs.e: 1 Timothy 3:1-7 details pastoral qualifications emphasizing moral integrity, family governance, teaching ability, and good reputation.

qs.q: In 2 Peter 1:5-7, Peter instructs believers to build a ladder of spiritual growth, adding to faith virtue, to virtue knowledge, to knowledge temperance, to temperance patience, to patience godliness, to godliness brotherly kindness, and to brotherly kindness
qs.e: 2 Peter 1:5-7 outlines the virtues of Christian character growth, culminating in 'charity' (agape love), ensuring spiritual fruitfulness.

qs.q: God commanded a disciple in Damascus named Ananias (Acts 9:10-15) to lay hands on Saul, revealing that Saul was
o: a chosen vessel unto Me, to bear My name before Gentiles, kings, and children of Israel
a spy sent by the Roman governor Pontius Pilate
a dangerous wolf who must be put on probation for seven years
a prophet assigned exclusively to the tribe of Benjamin
qs.e: Acts 9:15 records God's divine commission given to Ananias regarding Saul's apostolic calling to Gentiles, kings, and Israel.

qs.q: The primary issue resolved by the Jerusalem Council in Acts 15 was whether
o: the church headquarters should be relocated to Antioch
Paul should be recognized as an apostle equal to Peter
Jewish Christians should stop worshipping in the Jerusalem Temple
Gentile converts to Christianity were required to be circumcised and keep the Mosaic Law to be saved
qs.e: Acts 15:1-2 records the debate sparked by Judaizers in Antioch, which the Council resolved by ruling that Gentiles are saved by grace through faith without Mosaic circumcision.

qs.q: During Paul's Second Missionary Journey, what night vision prompted him to sail across into Europe (Acts 16:9)?
o: A sheet containing clean and unclean animals descending from heaven
A man of Macedonia standing and praying 'Come over into Macedonia, and help us'
An angel standing on the sea of Galilee pointing west
The prophet Agabus tying his hands with a belt
qs.e: Acts 16:9 describes the Macedonian Call, which opened Gospel expansion into Europe (Philippi, Thessalonica, Athens, Corinth).

qs.q: In 1 Corinthians 12, Paul uses the metaphor of the human body to teach that the Church is
o: a physical building constructed of literal stone and cedar wood
a strict hierarchy where prominent gifts despise lesser gifts
a unified spiritual body with diverse members possessing different gifts, all necessary for mutual flourishing
a collection of independent individuals with no accountability to one another
qs.e: 1 Corinthians 12:12-27 emphasizes unity in diversity: many members forming one body in Christ, each gift given by the Spirit for the common good.

qs.q: In Galatians 5:22-23, Paul lists the Fruit of the Spirit as love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness, faith, meekness, and
qs.e: Galatians 5:22-23 enumerates the ninefold Fruit of the Spirit, concluding with temperance (self-control), against which there is no law.

qs.q: In 2 Corinthians 5:17, Paul describes the spiritual reality of every believer in Christ by writing:
o: 'Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new'
'Therefore if any man be in Christ, he receives earthly political crowns'
'Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is exempt from all earthly trials'
'Therefore if any man be in Christ, he must keep the Mosaic ceremonial law'
qs.e: 2 Corinthians 5:17 asserts radical spiritual regeneration: union with Christ produces a new creation with old sinful patterns passing away.

qs.q: Why did God bless the seventh day and sanctify it according to Genesis 2:1-3?
o: To signal that God would never again intervene in earthly human history
Because He rested from all His work of creation, establishing a pattern for human rest
Because God required physical recuperation after exhausting His power
To establish a mandatory day of national military preparation
qs.e: Genesis 2:1-3 notes that God rested on the seventh day from all His work and sanctified it, creating a divine principle of Sabbath rest later embodied in the Fourth Commandment.

qs.q: When Adam was confronted by God after eating the forbidden fruit, his attempt to blame Eve demonstrated that sin immediately produced
o: relational fracture, self-justification, and a refusal to take personal responsibility
a desire to offer a sin offering on an altar
increased trust and unity between husband and wife
qs.e: In Genesis 3:12, Adam responded 'The woman whom thou gavest to be with me, she gave me of the tree, and I did eat,' illustrating how sin fractures relationships and produces blame-shifting.

qs.q: In Genesis 15, when God ratified His covenant with Abraham through divided animal pieces, the passing of the smoking oven and burning torch alone meant that
o: the covenant would terminate if Israel ever sinned in Canaan
Abraham was required to walk through the fire to prove his loyalty
God bound Himself unconditionally to fulfill His covenant promises to Abraham's offspring
the covenant depended entirely on human perfection and legal works
qs.e: In Genesis 15:17-18, the passing of God's presence (smoking furnace and burning lamp) through the pieces while Abram slept represented God's solemn, unconditional oath.

qs.q: What spiritual lesson is conveyed by Sarah's initial laughter when told she would bear a son in old age (Genesis 18)?
o: Human impossibility does not limit divine power and fulfillment of promise
Laughter is mandatory when receiving prophetic revelations
Angelic messengers must be tested by human wisdom before belief
Doubting God's word results in immediate cancellation of covenant blessings
qs.e: In Genesis 18:13-14, the Lord responded to Sarah's laughter by stating: 'Is any thing too hard for the LORD?', teaching that divine promises transcend natural human limitations.

qs.q: In Jacob's patriarchal blessing upon his sons in Genesis 49, the ruler's scepter was promised to reside with the tribe of
qs.e: Genesis 49:10 prophecies: 'The sceptre shall not depart from Judah, nor a lawgiver from between his feet, until Shiloh come; and unto him shall the gathering of the people be.'

qs.q: Before his death in Egypt, Joseph made the children of Israel swear an oath concerning his bones because he possessed
o: a desire to be worshipped as a god in the cave of Machpelah
distrust in his brothers' commitment to stay in Egypt
unshakable faith that God would surely visit them and bring them back to Canaan
fear that Egyptian embalmers would desecrate his burial tomb
qs.e: Genesis 50:24-25 and Hebrews 11:22 highlight Joseph's faith in God's covenant promise to return Israel to Canaan, requesting his bones be carried up during the Exodus.

qs.q: The mercy seat (Kaporet) situated upon the Ark of the Covenant inside the Holy of Holies represented
o: the physical resting chair reserved for the High Priest
the storage chest for Pharaoh's captured royal crown
the throne of God's presence where blood was sprinkled for national atonement
the altar where daily grain offerings were burnt by priests
qs.e: Exodus 25:21-22 and Leviticus 16 explain that the mercy seat above the Ark was where God met with Israel and where sacrificial blood was sprinkled on the Day of Atonement.

qs.q: Why was Moses forbidden by God from entering the Promised Land according to Numbers 20?
o: Because he struck the rock at Kadesh in anger instead of speaking to it as commanded, failing to hallow God
Because he refused to lead Israel against the Canaanite giants
Because he allowed the Golden Calf to be built at Sinai
Because he married a Cushite woman without Aaron's consent
qs.e: Numbers 20:11-12 states that Moses struck the rock twice in anger, misrepresenting God's holiness before Israel, causing God to declare he would not lead them into Canaan.

qs.q: The repeated phrase concluding the book of Judges ('In those days there was no king in Israel: every man did that which was right in his own eyes') highlights
o: the complete perfection of tribal self-governance
the necessity of abolishing the Mosaic Law
the moral and spiritual anarchy resulting from a lack of godly leadership and divine authority
the military superiority of Philistine city-states
qs.e: Judges 21:25 summarizes the period of the Judges as an era of spiritual chaos and moral relativism when people rejected God's righteous standards.

qs.q: Hannah's prayer at Shiloh in 1 Samuel 1 is significant in Israel's history because her vow led directly to
o: the establishment of the temple building in Jerusalem
the birth and consecration of Samuel, who bridged the period of Judges to the Monarchy
the elevation of Eli's sons Hophni and Phinehas as righteous judges
the immediate destruction of the Philistine temple of Dagon
qs.e: Hannah's passionate prayer and vow (1 Sam 1:11) resulted in Samuel's birth, who served as prophet, priest, and last judge, anointing Israel's first kings.

qs.q: What brought about King Solomon's spiritual downfall in his later years according to 1 Kings 11?
o: He allied with the Philistines against the tribe of Ephraim
His foreign wives turned his heart away after pagan gods like Ashtoreth, Chemosh, and Molech
He depleted the royal treasury through excessive military campaigns
He abandoned the Temple in Jerusalem and moved the ark to Samaria
qs.e: 1 Kings 11:4 states: 'For it came to pass, when Solomon was old, that his wives turned away his heart after other gods,' resulting in the division of the kingdom.

qs.q: David's deep genuine repentance following his adultery and murder is recorded scripturally in
o: Psalm 51, where he pleads for a clean heart and a right spirit
1 Kings 1, where he crowns Solomon at Gihon spring
1 Chronicles 29, where he donates gold for temple construction
Psalm 23, where he praises God as his Good Shepherd
qs.e: Psalm 51 was written by David after Nathan confronted him, reflecting profound sorrow, confession ('Against thee, thee only, have I sinned'), and plea for spiritual restoration.

qs.q: King Asa of Judah was commended as a godly reformer, yet in his old age he stumbled spiritually by
o: building high places for Baal inside Jerusalem
marrying the daughter of Ahab to consolidate power
relying on a military treaty with Ben-hadad of Syria instead of trusting Yahweh during a conflict with Baasha
executing the prophet Hanani for praising his military tactics
qs.e: 2 Chronicles 16:7-10 records Hanani rebuking Asa because he relied on the king of Syria rather than Yahweh, showing spiritual decline in Asa's later years.

qs.q: How did Ahijah the Shilonite symbolically depict the coming division of Solomon's kingdom to Jeroboam (1 Kings 11)?
o: He broke twelve clay pots before the city gates of Jerusalem
He poured out ten measures of oil on Jeroboam's head
He divided a golden crown into two unequal parts
He tore his new garment into twelve pieces and gave ten pieces to Jeroboam
qs.e: 1 Kings 11:30-31 records Ahijah tearing his new garment into twelve pieces and telling Jeroboam to take ten, signifying God giving him ten tribes.

qs.q: How did Elisha reward the hospitality of the prominent Shunammite woman who built a roof room for him?
o: He granted her family perpetual tax exemption in Israel
He secured a royal government pension for her husband
He prophesied that she would bear a son, and later raised that son from the dead
He healed her from a long-standing incurable blood disease
qs.e: 2 Kings 4:8-37 relates how Elisha promised her a child in her old age and later restored the child to life when he died of heatstroke in the harvest field.

qs.q: Elijah's challenge to the Israelites on Mount Carmel ('How long halt ye between two opinions?') challenged them regarding the sin of
o: failing to offer animal sacrifices at the annual feasts
syncretism, attempting to blend Yahweh worship with pagan Baal worship
neglecting the defense of their city walls
refusing to pay sanctuary tithes to the Levites
qs.e: In 1 Kings 18:21, Elijah rebuked the people's indecision and syncretism: 'If the LORD be God, follow him: but if Baal, then follow him,' demanding total allegiance.

qs.q: Ezra the scribe set his heart on a threefold ministry upon returning to Jerusalem (Ezra 7:10), which was to
o: consecrate high priests, offering animal sacrifices, and building high places
rebuild the city walls, train soldiers, and collect taxes
seek the Law of the LORD, do it, and teach in Israel statutes and judgments
crown Zerubbabel as king, execute false prophets, and defeat Samaritans
qs.e: Ezra 7:10 outlines Ezra's exemplary model of spiritual leadership: study ('seek'), practice ('do'), and instruction ('teach').

qs.q: How did King Hezekiah react when Sennacherib of Assyria sent a terrifying letter threatening Jerusalem's destruction (2 Kings 19)?
o: He ordered his generals to launch an immediate night attack
He sent secret envoys to hire Egyptian mercenaries
He went up to the Temple and spread the letter out before the LORD in prayer
He offered to surrender the city and go into Babylonian exile
qs.e: 2 Kings 19:14 records Hezekiah taking Sennacherib's blasphemous letter, spreading it before Yahweh in prayer, which resulted in divine deliverance.

qs.q: In Psalm 51, David's plea ('Create in me a clean heart, O God; and renew a right spirit within me') reveals that true repentance requires
o: offering thousands of rams in burnt sacrifice
internal spiritual transformation by God rather than mere outward ritual observance
building an elaborate stone altar in Jerusalem
donating half of one's kingdom to the Levites
qs.e: Psalm 51:10, 16-17 emphasizes that God does not delight in outward sacrifice alone, but in 'a broken and a contrite heart' and inner cleansing.

qs.q: The phrase 'Vanity of vanities, all is vanity' in Ecclesiastes 1:2 expresses the author's observation that
o: human intellectual study is a sin against divine revelation
human earthly accomplishments and pleasures are temporary and meaningless apart from God
God does not exist or care about earthly creation
the physical material universe is inherently evil and demonic
qs.e: Ecclesiastes uses 'vanity' (hebel - vapor/transience) to show that earthly goals pursued 'under the sun' without reference to God yield no lasting satisfaction.

qs.q: Jeremiah's prophecy of the New Covenant in Jeremiah 31:31-34 promises that God will
o: write His law upon their hearts and minds, granting divine forgiveness and personal knowledge of God
re-engrave the Ten Commandments on new stone tablets at Sinai
require mandatory animal sacrifices in every city across the earth
restore the physical monarchy of Saul over all twelve tribes
qs.e: Jeremiah 31:31-34 contrasts the Mosaic Covenant with the New Covenant, where God writes His law internally on human hearts and remembers sin no more.

qs.q: In Daniel 7, the vision of the four great beasts emerging from the sea represented human worldly empires, which were ultimately overcome by
o: the eternal, indestructible kingdom given to the 'Son of Man' and the saints of the Most High
the reinstatement of the Levitical high priesthood
the military alliance between Persia and Greece
a giant flood that covered the entire face of the earth
qs.e: Daniel 7:13-14 depicts the 'Son of man' coming with the clouds of heaven to receive an everlasting kingdom that shall not be destroyed.

qs.q: Haggai confronted the returned exiles in Jerusalem because they prioritized building their own paneled houses while
o: the house of the LORD (the Temple) lay in ruins and neglect
the Levites were begging for food in the market
the city walls were being attacked by Sanballat
the law of Moses was being burned by Persian officers
qs.e: Haggai 1:4 rebukes the returned exiles: 'Is it time for you, O ye, to dwell in your cieled houses, and this house lie waste?', calling them to put God's house first.

qs.q: In Malachi 3:8-10, God accused the post-exilic community of 'robbing God' through
o: sacrificing foreign idols on the high places
withholding tithes and offerings, promising open windows of heaven if they brought full tithes into the storehouse
stealing gold vessels from the sanctuary treasury
refusing to offer physical labor on the city walls
qs.e: Malachi 3:8-10 rebukes spiritual neglect in financial stewardship: 'Will a man rob God? Yet ye have robbed me... In tithes and offerings,' promising abundant blessing upon obedience.

qs.q: Why did Jesus insist on being baptized by John despite John's protestation ('I have need to be baptized of thee') in Matthew 3:15?
o: Because Jesus had personal sins that required ritual cleansing in the Jordan
To prove to the Sanhedrin that He was a loyal follower of John
To fulfill all righteousness by identifying with sinful humanity and inaugurating His public ministry
Because the Mosaic Law required every Jewish child to be immersed at age thirty
qs.e: Matthew 3:15 records Jesus saying: 'Suffer it to be so now: for thus it becometh us to fulfill all righteousness,' consecrating Himself for His messianic mission.

qs.q: The contrast between the announcement of Jesus' birth to humble shepherds in Luke 2 and to the Magi in Matthew 2 reveals that
o: the Gospel message transcends social and racial barriers, calling both poor outcasts and prominent Gentiles
Matthew wrote exclusively for Gentile audiences while Luke wrote for Jews
shepherds were spiritually superior to educated scholars in ancient Israel
Herod favored local shepherds over foreign eastern travelers
qs.e: Luke depicts poor Jewish shepherds receiving angelic revelation while Matthew records wealthy Gentile Magi following a star, illustrating the universal scope of the Gospel.

qs.q: In Matthew 5:43-48, Jesus commanded His followers to love their enemies and pray for their persecutors so that they may be
o: promoted to positions of authority in the Roman government
exempt from all physical suffering and persecution on earth
sons of their Father in heaven, who makes His sun rise on the evil and on the good
praised by Pharisees as righteous lawkeepers
qs.e: Matthew 5:44-45 teaches that radical love for enemies reflects God's impartial, gracious goodness, distinguishing Christians from worldly standards.

qs.q: What did Jesus mean when He asserted in Matthew 5:17 that He came 'not to destroy the law, or the prophets... but to fulfil'?
o: He came to accomplish their true intent, embody their prophetic types, and establish their moral perfection
He came to enforce every ceremonial sacrifice permanently upon Gentile converts
He came to replace the Ten Commandments with rabbinical traditions
He came to declare the Old Testament Scriptures obsolete and invalid
qs.e: Matthew 5:17-18 affirms the enduring authority of Scripture; Jesus fulfills the Law through His sinless life, substitutionary death, and deeper ethical revelation.

qs.q: What spiritual truth is illustrated by the attitude of the elder brother in the Parable of the Prodigal Son (Luke 15:25-32)?
o: Firstborn sons in Israel are entitled to twice as much inheritance
Fasting and religious obedience eliminate the need for celebratory feasts
Self-righteous legalism and envy can blind a person to the joy of grace and divine mercy shown to repentant sinners
Working faithfully in a father's field earns unconditional love
qs.e: The elder brother's resentment represents the self-righteous Pharisees who complained about Jesus receiving sinners, exposing a cold, loveless heart.

qs.q: The Parable of the Workers in the Vineyard (Matthew 20:1-16), where those hired at the eleventh hour received the same wage as those hired at daybreak, illustrates that
o: early workers are spiritually inferior to late converts
employers should violate agreed employment contracts with laborers
God's salvation and reward operate by sovereign, generous grace rather than human concepts of merit
hard physical labor yields no reward in God's kingdom
qs.e: Matthew 20:14-15 reveals God's sovereign grace: 'Is it not lawful for me to do what I will with mine own? Is thine eye evil, because I am good?', defying human merit-based pride.

qs.q: In John 9, when Jesus healed the man born blind by anointed his eyes with clay and sending him to wash in Siloam, the Pharisees rejected the miracle primarily because
o: the man born blind was not a resident of Jerusalem
Jesus performed the miracle on the Sabbath day, violating their strict Sabbath traditions
clay was considered ceremonial unclean material
the pool of Siloam was controlled by Roman soldiers
qs.e: John 9:16 shows the Pharisees' legalistic blindness: 'This man is not of God, because he keepeth not the sabbath day,' ignoring the undeniable miracle.

qs.q: Why did Peter begin to sink after walking on the water toward Jesus in Matthew 14:28-31?
o: Because he shifted his focus from Jesus to the boisterous wind and became afraid
Because his disciples pulled him down into the water
Because Jesus commanded him to return to the boat
Because a sudden wave struck him from behind
qs.e: Matthew 14:30 notes: 'when he saw the wind boisterous, he was afraid; and beginning to sink, he cried, saying, Lord, save me,' illustrating the danger of taking eyes off Christ.

qs.q: The Roman centurion guarding the cross at Jesus' death exclaimed 'Truly this was the Son of God' (Matthew 27:54) after witnessing
o: the High Priest falling dead in front of the cross
the earthquake, the darkness, and the majestic way Jesus expired on the cross
an angelic army descending from heaven to destroy Pilate's soldiers
Jesus physically stepping down from the cross alive
qs.e: Matthew 27:54 records that the centurion and soldiers feared greatly after seeing the earthquake and cosmic signs, testifying to Jesus' divine Sonship.

qs.q: How did Jesus restore Peter following Peter's three denials (John 21:15-17)?
o: By re-baptizing him in the Sea of Tiberias
By stripped him of his apostolic title for three years
By requiring him to fast forty days in the wilderness
By asking him three times 'Lovest thou me?' and commissioning him to feed His sheep
qs.e: John 21:15-17 records Jesus asking Peter three times if he loved Him, mirroring his three denials and graciously reinstating him to pastoral care ('Feed my lambs', 'Feed my sheep').

qs.q: How did the severe persecution following Stephen's martyrdom paradoxically advance the Gospel (Acts 8:1-4)?
o: It scattered believers throughout Judea and Samaria, and they went everywhere preaching the word
It forced the Sanhedrin to convert to Christianity
It brought an immediate end to Jewish animal sacrifices
It led the Roman governor to declare Christianity a legal religion
qs.e: Acts 8:4 shows divine providence at work: persecution scattered the seed of the Gospel beyond Jerusalem into Judea and Samaria.

qs.q: When Rhoda told the praying disciples in Mary's house that Peter was standing at the outer gate (Acts 12:13-15), their initial unbelieving reaction was
o: 'Open the gate immediately to welcome him'
'Thou art mad... It is his angel'
qs.e: Acts 12:15 illustrates human weakness in prayer: even while praying for Peter's release, they found his actual standing at the door unbelievable.

qs.q: The immediate result of Philip's personal evangelism with the Ethiopian eunuch along the desert road was that the eunuch
o: invited Philip to accompany him permanently to Ethiopia as a court priest
returned to Jerusalem to offer sacrifices at the Temple
refused to believe without seeing a physical sign
confessed faith in Jesus Christ as the Son of God and was immediately baptized in water
qs.e: Acts 8:36-38 describes the eunuch asking 'what doth hinder me to be baptized?', confessing faith, and being immersed by Philip before going on his way rejoicing.

qs.q: When Paul was tried before King Agrippa II and Festus at Caesarea (Acts 26), Agrippa responded to Paul's impassioned Gospel appeal by saying:
o: 'This man has committed a capital crime worthy of immediate execution'
'Almost thou persuadest me to be a Christian'
'I will release thee if thou payest a sum of gold'
'Thou art mad; much learning doth make thee mad'
qs.e: Acts 26:28 records Agrippa's famous reply: 'Almost thou persuadest me to be a Christian,' while Festus charged him with madness (v.24).

qs.q: Why was Paul transported to Rome as a prisoner despite both Festus and Agrippa admitting he had done nothing worthy of death or bonds (Acts 26:32)?
o: Because Paul had exercised his legal right as a Roman citizen to appeal his case directly unto Caesar
Because Roman law required all religious leaders to be tried in Rome
Because a prophet commanded him to stay bound for seven years
Because the Sanhedrin paid Festus to keep Paul in chains permanently
qs.e: Acts 25:11 & 26:32 note that Agrippa stated Paul might have been set at liberty if he had not appealed unto Caesar, fulfilling God's plan for Paul to witness in Rome.

qs.q: In Romans 6:1-4, Paul refutes the false charge that grace encourages sinful living by explaining that Christian baptism signifies
o: being buried with Christ into death, so that just as Christ was raised, we also should walk in newness of life
an outward social initiation into Jewish culture
a guarantee of physical immunity from earthly death
a simple ceremonial wash that permits believers to sin freely without penalty
qs.e: Romans 6:1-4 asserts that genuine faith unites the believer to Christ's death and resurrection, rendering living in deliberate sin a theological impossibility.

qs.q: In Colossians 1:15-18, Paul exalts the supreme preeminence of Jesus Christ by declaring Him to be
o: the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of every creature, by whom all things were created and consist
a high angelic created spirit subordinate to Michael
a human prophet who achieved divine consciousness through meditation
one of several divine avatars sent to guide humanity
qs.e: Colossians 1:15-18 affirms Christ's absolute deity, creator status, and headship over all creation and the Church.

qs.q: In Revelation 2-3, the messages to the Seven Churches of Asia constantly conclude with a specific divine promise to
qs.e: Each of the seven letters in Revelation 2-3 (Ephesus, Smyrna, Pergamum, Thyatira, Sardis, Philadelphia, Laodicea) promises eternal rewards specifically 'to him that overcometh'.

qs.q: Revelation 21:1-4 describes the ultimate hope of Christian living in the New Jerusalem, where God will dwell with His people and
o: the Mosaic ceremonial sacrifices will be re-established forever
human beings will become independent gods ruling separate planets
God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes; and there shall be no more death, neither sorrow, nor crying, neither shall there be any more pain
believers will return to mortal earthly existence under Roman rule
qs.e: Revelation 21:3-4 provides the glorious vision of eternal consummation: God dwelling with humanity, banishing death, suffering, and sorrow forever.

qs.q: In Hebrews 4:14-16, believers are encouraged to come boldly unto the throne of grace because Jesus our High Priest
o: requires angelic intercessors to carry human petitions to God
is unconcerned with earthly human temptations and weaknesses
demands expensive animal sacrifices before listening to prayer
was in all points tempted like as we are, yet without sin, and can be touched with the feeling of our infirmities
qs.e: Hebrews 4:15-16 points to Christ's empathetic, sinless High Priesthood, inviting believers to receive mercy and grace to help in time of need.

qs.q: In James 3:2-12, the tongue is compared to a small bit in a horse's mouth and a small rudder on a ship to illustrate
o: the physical organs required for vocal psalm singing
that human speech cannot be judged by God
how a small organ possesses immense power to direct and defile the entire human life
the necessity of learning foreign Greek languages
qs.e: James 3 illustrates the disproportionate power of speech: a tiny organ that can cause vast destruction if uncontrolled, requiring divine wisdom.

qs.q: In 1 John 4:7-8, John urges Christians to love one another because love is of God, and everyone that loveth is born of God, for
o: love eliminates the need for repentance
qs.e: 1 John 4:7-8 states the fundamental nature of God: 'God is love', making Christian brotherly love the essential mark of divine sonship.

qs.q: When the crowd asked Peter and the apostles what they must do after Peter's Pentecost sermon (Acts 2:38), Peter instructed:
o: 'Join the Zealot movement to overthrow Rome'
'Flee from Jerusalem to the mountains of Judea'
'Repent, and be baptized every one of you in the name of Jesus Christ for the remission of sins'
'Offer burnt sacrifices in the Temple according to the law'
qs.e: Acts 2:38 records Peter's clear apostolic gospel response: 'Repent, and be baptized every one of you in the name of Jesus Christ for the remission of sins, and ye shall receive the gift of the Holy Ghost.'

qs.q: In Joppa, Peter raised from the dead a godly disciple known for her abundant good works and acts of charity named
qs.e: Acts 9:36-41 records Peter praying over dead Tabitha (Dorcas) in Joppa, saying 'Tabitha, arise,' restoring her alive to the saints and widows.

qs.q: When King Herod Agrippa I imprisoned Peter in Jerusalem (Acts 12), how was Peter released on the night before his execution?
o: An angel of the Lord struck off his chains and led him safely past the guards
The church paid a ransom to Herod's soldiers
A sudden earthquake destroyed the prison walls
Roman soldiers mutinied against Herod's command
qs.e: Acts 12:7-10 relates the miraculous deliverance of Peter by an angel while the church prayed fervently at Mary's house.

qs.q: Stephen, one of the seven deacons, was accused by false witnesses before the Sanhedrin (Acts 6) of speaking blasphemous words against
o: the school of Gamaliel and the scribes
the city walls and gates of Jerusalem
the Roman Emperor Caesar and Pontius Pilate
this holy place (the Temple) and the law of Moses
qs.e: Acts 6:13-14 records false witnesses charging Stephen: 'This man ceaseth not to speak blasphemous words against this holy place, and the law.'

qs.q: While being stoned to death by the Jewish council, Stephen cried out with his dying breath:
o: 'May fire from heaven consume my persecutors'
'Lord, lay not this sin to their charge'
'I appeal my case to Caesar in Rome'
'Revenge my blood upon this wicked generation'
